Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the Afghan Taliban's use of drones, particularly in light of the Houthis' use of the technology against Saudi Arabia, DG ISPR said the character of warfare had changed and the military was adapting accordingly.

He stated that the army was preparing for developments in both contact and non-contact warfare, including cyber operations, drones and long-range munitions, while assessing the capabilities needed to address present and future challenges.

He added that the proliferation of non-contact warfare capabilities among non-state actors, including the Taliban, groups referred to as Khawarij and the Houthis, posed a threat to all countries. "These states will have to reconsider and re-evaluate their security architecture," he said.

Asked whether he feared a situation similar to that between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia developing between Afghanistan and Pakistan, he said Afghanistan's drone capabilities were not indigenous.

"There is no drone industry, there is no technology of that sort in Afghanistan. So it's been provided by the sponsors, the terror sponsors, because the biggest terror sponsor here is India," he said.

He alleged that the Afghan Taliban were acting as India's proxy in the context of terrorism in Pakistan.

Referring to the previous conflict with India, he said New Delhi had sent dozens of sophisticated drones, which Pakistani forces had brought down.

"So we are much ahead where we stand in our own operational readiness," he said, adding that Afghanistan could attempt to send drones but Pakistan had the capability to intercept them.

He also said Afghanistan could not absorb the retaliation Pakistan was capable of delivering.

Asked whether Pakistan's military used artificial intelligence to identify targets, as well as other emerging technologies, Lt Gen Chaudhry said the army was incorporating all technologies required to keep pace with the changing nature of warfare.

He said the rapid transformation of warfare and the pace at which new technologies were being introduced meant professional armies could not afford to fall behind.

However, he declined to discuss specific applications of artificial intelligence, quantum technology and cyber capabilities, saying he could not disclose how the military was using them.

"We use all technologies, absorbing all sorts of technologies that are essential in the changing character of war," he said.

"We are using all sorts of technologies. We are a technology-savvy army," he added.

He again alleged that the Afghan Taliban's drone capabilities had been provided by their sponsors, particularly India, arguing that Afghanistan had neither a drone industry nor technology of its own.

Lt Gen Chaudhry also described India as the "prime contractor" behind militant groups operating against Pakistan, with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) acting as its proxies.

Responding to reports that the Afghan Taliban had accused Pakistan of hosting anti-Taliban elements and coordinating former Afghan government generals and other groups opposed to the regime, he rejected the allegations and accused the Taliban of using non-state actors, militias and mercenaries to pursue their objectives.

"So that's how you play the victim card. They are apt in using non-state actors, militias, mercenaries for their objectives. So they think everyone does that," he said.

"We are a state. Afghanistan is not a state. Afghanistan is still being run by a non-state actor. It's a regime."

He said decades of foreign intervention by the Soviet Union and the United States had allowed multiple agencies and proxy groups to establish roots in Afghanistan. The country, he added, had experienced more than 40 years of foreign interventions, making its situation different from that of Pakistan and other states.

"The forces have gone physically, but still that front of Afghan Taliban is a proxy to multiple parties," he said.

He said the presence of these groups was not merely his assessment but was also reflected in United Nations reports and intelligence assessments by the United States and several other countries.

"How could so many terrorist organisations, the whole alphabet, thrive over there?" he asked.

Questioning the credibility of allegations made by the Afghan Taliban, he cited previous claims by the regime that a person picked up from a street in Kabul was a Pakistani pilot captured in Shalwar Kameez and that Pakistani tanks had been seized.

"It's the same regime which the world has seen, some day picked up a random person from the street in Kabul and said this is a Pakistani pilot that we have captured in Shalwar Kameez. It's the same regime that paraded its own tanks in the streets and said that we have captured Pakistani tanks," he said.

He said Pakistan had drawn conclusions from its experience and believed that armed groups, militias and mercenaries could not be tolerated in any state.

Asked whether isolating the Taliban would help Afghanistan, particularly amid concerns about the impact of the opium ban and reduced foreign assistance to farmers, Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan was not advocating the country's isolation.

Instead, he said, the international community and regional countries should ask the Taliban authorities to act like a state and stop producing opium and supporting militant groups.

"Afghanistan is producing right now; it has only two products: terrorism and drugs. And both are not good for the world and the region and everyone," he said.

He stressed that engagement with Afghanistan was necessary and said Pakistan was also engaging with the authorities in Kabul. However, he said Islamabad demanded that Afghan territory should not be used to support terrorism inside Pakistan.

"We only ask you that don't support terrorism inside Pakistan. Stop harbouring the terrorist leaders," he said.

He alleged that militant groups operating inside Pakistan received their instructions and weapons from Afghanistan. He also claimed that Afghan citizens, including personnel of the Afghan Taliban regime, had been found among militant formations targeted by Pakistani forces.

"We ask them not to do it. If you do it, then there will be a cost, and we are capable of imposing that cost," he said, adding that Pakistan had a clear strategy for imposing such a cost.

The remarks came amid strained relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan due to recurring cross-border terrorism and security concerns. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Afghan Taliban administration to prevent terrorist organisations, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), from using its territory to launch attacks inside Pakistan.

A day earlier, the Information Ministry maintained that the Taliban regime’s continued refusal to address terrorism was the principal barrier to normal relations and took issue with Kabul’s characterisation of the matter.

“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” the statement said.

Pakistan maintains that the terrorist nexus extended beyond the movement of terrorists across the border to their training, arming and operational support.

Security officials estimate that up to 70 per cent of the Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists infiltrating Pakistan were of Afghan origin. They further claim that the Taliban regime had allowed leftover US and NATO weapons to reach terrorist groups, including Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan.

The security establishment also linked the escalation in attacks to the presence of terrorist infrastructure inside Afghanistan.

In 2026 alone, terrorism emanating from Afghan soil claimed the lives of 1,327 Pakistanis and injured another 2,484, according to figures cited by Pakistani authorities.

Officials said that whenever Pakistani forces targeted terrorist hideouts, the Taliban regime instead moved to defend the militants and their sanctuaries rather than dismantling the infrastructure. The issue, Pakistan has argued, was not confined to TTP.

UN assessments have continued to document the presence of several other militant organisations in Afghanistan, including al Qaeda, the East Turkestan Islamic Movement and Islamic State-Khorasan, reinforcing concerns about the broader militant ecosystem operating from Afghan territory.

headline: Petit Planet brings Animal Crossing competition to Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027
description: HoYoverse confirms 2027 Nintendo Switch 2 release for its upcoming life simulation game Petit Planet
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
HoYoverse confirms 2027 Nintendo Switch 2 release for its upcoming life simulation game Petit Planet

HoYoverse's upcoming life simulation game Petit Planet is heading to Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027, setting up a potential competitor to Nintendo's Animal Crossing series on the console.

The announcement was made during a pre-launch special programme livestream hosted by HoYoverse.

A brief trailer at the end of the presentation confirmed that a Switch 2 version is in development, alongside gameplay footage showing the game running in both docked and handheld modes.

Petit Planet is already scheduled to launch on PC, iOS and Android on December 4 2026. The newly confirmed console version will follow in 2027, although HoYoverse has not provided a more specific release date.

The game shares several features with Animal Crossing: New Horizons, including character customisation and developing a homestead.

However, rather than building a traditional island community, players work towards creating and developing their own planet. Its science-fiction setting also gives it a different visual identity.

Farming is expected to play a more prominent role in Petit Planet than in Animal Crossing, with the game also drawing comparisons to other cosy simulation titles such as Stardew Valley.

The upcoming release could give Nintendo Switch 2 owners another option in the life simulation genre.

headline: Crew from NASA's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
description: Four entered a simulated Mars habitat in 2025, growing crops and testing delayed communications
author: Reuters
article_text:
The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation ​at the US space agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston, an endeavor designed to help prepare for a ‌possible future excursion by NASA astronauts to Earth's planetary neighbor.

"It's been a hell of a year — analog astronauts living in captivity of our own free will," Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA, mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Center after ​emerging with her three crewmates on Saturday.

The four entered the 1,700-square-foot (158-square-meter) 3D-printed habitat on October 19, 2025, and performed ​tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with NASA officials with delays ⁠recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications.

NASA, which has explored Mars with robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft, has ambitions for a human mission ​to Mars as early as the 2030s, with plans before that to return astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972.

"We ​have a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain US preeminence in space," Ellis said.

Ellis mentioned the service academy for space-related operations pursued by President Donald Trump's administration and plans for a lunar base.

"Let's seize the initiative, lead with science that will benefit our economy and ensure our legacy in space for our ​children's children," Ellis said.

The other crew members were mission commander Ross Elder, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer.

"For ​Mars, the risks are great," Elder said in remarks after emerging from isolation. "But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work ‌and ⁠incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable."

The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with NASA scientists. NASA has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, ​and connected.

This was NASA's second ​CHAPEA mission, with another four-person ⁠crew in isolation at Johnson Space Center for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024.

Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Center, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation. Wyche said they ​managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.

Wyche also ​noted how the ⁠crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses.

"These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence — qualities that will be essential for future astronauts traveling millions of miles from home," Wyche said.

Wyche said the lessons learned from ⁠the CHAPEA ​crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first ​to the moon and "one day, Mars."

headline: Can Pakistan cash in on its diplomatic clout?
description: Can Pakistan cash in on its diplomatic clout?
author: Kamran Yousaf
article_text:
Pakistan's growing diplomatic and strategic clout is no longer in question. The more important question now is whether the country can turn that influence into something tangible at home. That may sound like an unusual way to judge foreign policy. But Pakistan has been here before. Its geography, military strength and relationships with major powers have repeatedly made it relevant during wars, crises and geopolitical realignments. What has remained elusive is the ability to convert that relevance into lasting economic gains.

The current situation offers another opportunity. Pakistan today has strong ties with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye under the Makkah pact while retaining an important relationship with Iran. At the same time, its ties with the US have seen a marked improvement. Islamabad is also involved in efforts to find a diplomatic way out of the Iran-US confrontation. The recent Tehran meeting involving Field Marshal Asim Munir, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin underlined how much the regional equation has changed. Pakistan is no longer trying simply to navigate the traditional Saudi-Iran rivalry. It is working with countries across those old divides. The Makkah pact has added another dimension. What began as a collective defence arrangement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could potentially evolve into something wider. Pakistani officials have publicly indicated that there is no bar on other countries, including Iran, joining the arrangement provided there is political agreement.

There is little doubt that all this has enhanced Pakistan's diplomatic relevance. But relevance alone does not pay the bills. This is where Islamabad needs to look beyond the immediate diplomatic gains. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries have long been crucial sources of remittances and financial support for Pakistan. Whenever Islamabad has faced a balance-of-payments crisis, friendly countries have stepped in with deposits, deferred oil facilities and other assistance. That model has run its course. If Pakistan now enjoys greater political capital in Riyadh, Ankara and Washington, it should be asking how that can translate into investment, market access, technology, jobs and greater trade.

The objective cannot simply be another deposit at the State Bank or another bailout. There is an uncomfortable domestic reality that makes this question even more urgent. The latest World Bank assessment shows Pakistan's national poverty rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. Around 70 million Pakistanis are estimated to be living in poverty. Across the border, India has moved in the opposite direction. World Bank data shows that poverty there has fallen significantly over the past decade. India has its own inequalities and enormous development challenges, but the direction of travel matters.

For Pakistan, that contrast should be sobering. For years, we have taken pride in the country's ability to punch above its weight internationally. There is some justification for that. Few countries with Pakistan's economic vulnerabilities could maintain relationships with Saudi Arabia, Iran, Türkiye, China, Russia and the US at the same time, particularly in such a polarised geopolitical environment. But there is also something fundamentally wrong when a country's external influence continues to outstrip its economic performance at home.

Foreign policy cannot be detached from that reality. Ultimately, its success cannot be measured only by access to powerful capitals, mediation efforts or Pakistan's seat at important regional tables. It must also create economic opportunities for the country it is meant to serve. Pakistan has diplomatic capital today. It should use it while the opportunity lasts. Because if poverty continues to rise, growth remains anaemic and millions of young Pakistanis struggle to find decent jobs, the distinction between foreign policy success and national success will become increasingly difficult to ignore.

headline: The Afghan mess
description: The Afghan mess
author: editorial
article_text:
The Afghan Taliban's tendency to blame Pakistan for deteriorating bilateral relations is nothing but an excuse to hide behind political exigency. The fact is that the reclusive regime in Kabul is squarely responsible for looking the other way as terror groups operate with impunity from Afghan soil. This complicity has been documented by the UN and various human rights bodies, which have called upon the militia to act with the decency expected of a sovereign state by shunning radicalism. Thus, the allegations repeated by Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid - claiming that Islamabad's "wrong policies" prevent a resolution to the conflict - amount to nothing more than sham politics.

For decades, Pakistan has stood at the vanguard of combating terrorism both at home and abroad. It has consistently engaged in every major dialogue process with the Taliban since their return to power in August 2021, driven by the hope that Kabul would commit to normalising bilateral relations. It is deeply concerning, however, that the Taliban regime routinely views non-state actors through a highly politicised lens, choosing to treat them as indispensable allies of the past. This misplaced loyalty lies at the heart of the current friction, providing a free pass to groups like Al-Qaeda, ISKP and TTP to operate with total impunity and launch deadly, cross-border operations.

Islamabad was entirely justified in reminding Kabul that "shifting blame, making hollow assurances, and questioning Pakistan's policies will neither resolve the crisis nor absolve Kabul of its responsibilities." The need of the hour is to view security through a shared prism of regionalism. This demands that Kabul halt cross-border provocations against Pakistani check-posts, cease deploying drones, and stop allowing terror cells to launch deadly rampages across the border. Meanwhile, the assertion by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Washington will evaluate the situation and intervene is too little, too late. The region is still reeling from the hasty, chaotic withdrawal of American forces from Afghanistan, an exit that left behind billions of dollars in military hardware and a shattered civil edifice.

headline: Fields of smoke
description: Fields of smoke
author: editorial
article_text:
Punjab's annual battle against smog cannot be won through fines or emergency measures alone. Every winter, the province finds itself confronting the same public health crisis with deteriorating air quality. Yet the persistence of crop-residue burning suggests that the authorities have failed to address one of the major contributors to this recurring emergency.

The latest satellite findings indicate that agricultural fires in Pakistan's Punjab now considerably outnumber those across the border in India, despite years of official campaigns against the practice. According to an environmental monitoring platform HamariHawa, Nasa satellites detected 13,241 fire spots in Pakistan's Punjab between October 1 and 29, compared with 3,158 in Indian Punjab. An estimated 92% of these detections were on farmland, suggesting widespread crop burning. These figures demand serious reflection on the measures and policies that have been adopted, particularly when the neighbouring province has demonstrated that substantial reductions are possible. The Punjab government has deployed 67 Quick Response Units but the detection of thousands of fires within a matter of days raises questions about the effectiveness of these arrangements. The underlying problem is that crop burning remains an economically convenient option. Many cannot afford specialised machinery, while others lack access to equipment capable of managing agricultural residue efficiently. The government must recognise that punitive measures, however necessary, cannot succeed without practical alternatives.

There is also an urgent need to improve transparency and accountability. Satellite monitoring should be accompanied by district-wise reporting that allows the public to assess whether enforcement measures are producing results. Authorities should identify persistent hotspots and investigate why burning continues in these areas. Without reliable public data, government's claims of progress will remain difficult to substantiate.

headline: Renewed hopes
description: Renewed hopes
author: editorial
article_text:
Pakistan's thrilling triumph in the ODI tri-series, also featuring heavyweight England and promising Sri Lanka, is a major turning point. The victory in the final fight against Sri Lankans at Gaddafi Stadium Lahore over the weekend marks the team's first tri-series title since 2008. For a cricket-loving nation desperate for consistent wins, this trophy brings more than just silverware - it brings real hope for a bright future. The historic win was built on a perfect mix of exciting young players and experienced veterans, proving that Pakistan is finally learning how to win consistently on the world stage.

The best part of this tournament was the rise of fresh talent. New batters like Hassan Nawaz, Saad Baig and Maaz Sadaqat played without fear, while all-rounder Arafat Minhas brought great energy to the squad. These young players proved they can handle pressure when it matters most. Alongside steady performances from Salman Ali Agha, this group of youngsters gives Pakistan the team balance and depth it has lacked for a very long time.

At the same time, Pakistan's world-class stars stood strong. The fast-bowling trio of Shaheen Shah Afridi, Haris Rauf and Naseem Shah worked together perfectly to destroy opposition batting lineups. Even leg-spinner Shadab Khan, who has most sat on the bench during the tournament, stepped up to save the team in a league match, hitting an incredible century to win a seemingly lost game. His stunning performance proves his immense value with the bat and highlights just how strong and promising Pakistan's bench depth has become.

The final match, meanwhile, belonged to veteran Fakhar Zaman. Chasing a challenging target of 326 runs, the left-handed batter scored a brilliant century – 127 off 99 balls studded with 11 fours and 6 sixes - which made the impossible chase look easy. This tournament shows that when Pakistan's experienced stars lead the way and the youth play freely, the team can beat anyone. This victory should not be a one-time celebration, but the start of a dominant new era.

headline: Suffix that reflects the zeitgeist
description: Suffix that reflects the zeitgeist
author: M Nadeem Nadir
article_text:
This is the age of maximisation: maximising looks, maximising the lucre, maximising social biome, maximising brownie points, or maximising what we are not. This maximising mentality is so ubiquitous that Dictionary.com has declared Maxxing the word of the year 2026. Addition of an extra X – not to please Elon Musk – in the word is reflective of going no-holds-barred on whatever activity we get involved in.

The suffix has roots in the gamification term, min-maxxing -- a gaming strategy wherein players maximise useful attributes and minimise weaknesses to create the most effective character. In October 2025, Nitsuh Abebe wrote an article, 'The Suffix That Tells Us to Ruthlessly Optimise Everything' and traced the origin or over-use of this suffix in video gaming: "It's how we got maxxing of just any personal quality, as if spending points in a video game skills tree."

Maxxing is the digital world's slang suffix, hence written as -maxxing, which means 'optimising one part of your life as far as it will go.' It is also reserved for describing Gen Z exuberance: pushing a specific area of life to its extreme limit. Staple it behind any noun to denote the hectic pursuit of anything. It serves as a classic example to understand how the online world intrudes into offline human life.

One of the strongest psychological explanations of unhealthy maxxing is perfectionism. Another explanation is that it is dominantly driven by constantly comparing ourselves with others. 'The suffix turns any mundane habit into a fake quest line.' Maxxing connotes improvement, becoming an addiction.

Let's touch upon its grammatical nuances. Verb: I am sleepmaxxing this weekend. Adjective: Make it your routine to have a protein-maxxed breakfast daily. Noun: She is an obsessed looks-maxxer. 'Looks-maxxing' best describes the zeitgeist of this age, which means to super-focus on improving our physical appearance. The term became a buzzword on online appearance forums in the early 2010s. That's where the term originates. The appendages of super, hyper, turbo or ultra are the part of this aberration.

Here are a few interesting terms suffixed with '-maxxing'. Vocabulary-maxxing: a craze among the young learners of a second language to amass as many a word-meaning as an obsession. Smell-maxxing connotes optimising fragrance to control how others perceive us. Gym-maxxing or personality-maxxing: the raison detre of modern lifestyle. Cozy-maxxing: a sedentary lifestyle ending upon making couch potatoes. Bribemaxxing, now you yourselves make it out, and that too in our context. Eyes rolled. Abebe says, "The suffix can still capture real strategic choices like MAGAmaxxing." Use the template and form CM-maxxing, Kaptaan-maxxing, or Party-maxxing to encapsulate our political cults.

Our education system can be summarised using the suffix -maxxing. Studying has become marksmaxxing: the rat race our students participate in. Degree-maxxing: amassing academic credentials without acquiring any professional competence. Tokenmaxxing: using AI as much as possible, especially in the context of doing one's job. Info-maxxing: collecting bits of information on socials to self-deceive that we are using social media constructively. Highly informed but poorly educated.

With such linguistic forays, the debate on the inclusion of slang in the main dictionaries ensues. As second language learners, we apprehend the inclusion as something compounding our language learning woes. Slang is purely a cultural entity. English, being the lingua franca, must consider its status before offering space to a slang entry. Linguist Vanessa Croft says digital media make language move at "warp speed", even faster than radio, film or television ever did. As swiftly as new terms catch on in the lexicon, they can just as quickly fall out of favour. "By the time millennials and Gen X or Gen Y start using the terms, Gen Z and Gen Alpha aren't using those terms anymore," she says.

"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. The suffix also pokes fun at ourselves when optimising our lives starts to feel absurd.

headline: Israel deadlocked
description: Israel deadlocked
author: Adeela Naureen, Waqar K Kauravi
article_text:
The votes have been counted, the exit polls have been dissected, and the spin rooms have done their work. And what has Israel's October 27 election actually produced? A nation more divided than ever, a political system more paralysed than before, and a prime minister who managed to survive but not to win.

Netanyahu's right-wing bloc is down from last elections performance but has denied the opposition a decisive majority. The election that was supposed to be a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership after the catastrophic security failures of October 7, 2023 ended in a virtual tie. Neither bloc can muster the 61 seats needed to govern. The country is split down the middle, and the fundamental question of who should lead it remains unanswered.

Netanyahu's Likud remains the largest single party with around 25 seats, but the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party is close behind with 23-24 seats. When grouped into blocs, the picture is even starker: Netanyahu's right-wing and religious parties command approximately 53 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu opposition holds roughly 48. Neither side comes close to the 61-seat threshold.

The high turnout, nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, reflected intense public engagement and a genuine desire for change. Yet the result showed a nation politically split down the middle, unable or unwilling to deliver a decisive verdict on its longest-serving leader.

What makes this impasse even more remarkable is the position of the Arab parties, which are projected to win a record 18-19 seats. Suddenly, they find themselves in a potential kingmaker role, even though both major blocs had ruled out including them in a coalition. This is the paradox of Israeli politics: the Arab minority can influence the outcome but cannot participate in governance. Their electoral strength is real, but their political power remains illusory.

Netanyahu knows he has not won. He has survived, barely, and he knows that his survival depends on forces beyond his control. Facing an ICC arrest warrant and domestic corruption charges, he has immense personal incentive to cling to power. He also hinted at a potential regional escalation involving Iran, a move that could shift the political dynamic or delay coalition talks. This is not statesmanship; it is survival tactics dressed up as leadership.

Eisenkot ran a campaign centered on accountability and integrity. His personal story, a bereaved father whose son fell in Gaza, a Mizrahi Jew from a demographic that typically leans right, gave him a unique appeal.

Eisenkot's allegations during the campaign were specific and damning. He accused Netanyahu of using national security for political survival, citing the prime minister's posting of AI-generated images of a nuclear bomb over Tel Aviv on election eve as "hysterical" fearmongering. He blamed Netanyahu of trying to sabotage the electoral process by attempting to meet with the police commissioner on election eve to discuss so-called election integrity issues. He targeted Netanyahu of failing to achieve the stated war objectives, pointing out that the promise of "total victory" had yielded nothing but a shift from "total victory" to "not surrendering".

These are not minor disagreements. They are fundamental indictments of a leader who, according to his challenger, has put his personal survival above the national interest.

Eisenkot's path to the premiership is mathematically possible but politically fraught. To become prime minister, he would need 61 seats. With his bloc at roughly 51-53 seats, he would need the outside support or inclusion of the Arab parties. But Eisenkot had explicitly ruled out governing with Arab parties during the campaign, and Netanyahu was already using this as a scare tactic, claiming such a government would lack legitimacy.

This leaves Eisenkot with two options, both deeply problematic. He could attempt a narrow minority government relying on Arab parties to abstain from key votes, a fragile arrangement that could collapse at any moment. Or he could form a unity government with Likud, a national emergency government that many in the opposition reject but which might be forced by the stalemate.

Both options are bad. The first is unstable and vulnerable to Netanyahu's scare tactics. The second requires Eisenkot to govern alongside the man he has accused of sabotaging democracy and failing the nation. Neither represents the change that the electorate apparently wanted.

Other two options are equally unstable, continuing with the stalemate leading to another election or Netanyahu trying to break Eisenkot allies to form another lose government.

Amid all the horse-race analysis and coalition arithmetic, a deeper truth is being overlooked. The strong showing of Arab-majority parties does not signal a fundamental shift in Israel's political direction or its approach to the Palestinians. This is a caution against overreading the election results. Even if Arab-led parties win more seats, the structural and ideological makeup of Israeli politics, particularly the dominance of right-wing and security-focused blocs remains intact. Those who see in these results evidence of a moderating or transforming Israel are engaging in wishful thinking. The election confirmed that the country remains evenly divided between those who want Netanyahu gone and those who still trust him to manage the country's security. It did not resolve the fundamental question of Israel's leadership. It merely confirmed that the country is stuck.

With final results due on November 4, the nation faces weeks of intense bargaining. Netanyahu, facing legal peril and political isolation, has every incentive to cling to power and to escalate regional tensions if it serves his interests. Eisenkot has warned him not to use security for political ends, stating: "Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs." But warnings are not constraints.

The election did not resolve Israel's leadership crisis. It did not deliver a verdict on October 7. It did not produce a government. It produced a stalemate, and stalemates in Israeli politics tend to favour the incumbent, especially one as skilled at survival as Netanyahu.

So, what's the final verdict. Not a victory. Not a change. Just a deadlock, and a nation waiting to see what happens next.

article_html:
The votes have been counted, the exit polls have been dissected, and the spin rooms have done their work. And what has Israel's October 27 election actually produced? A nation more divided than ever, a political system more paralysed than before, and a prime minister who managed to survive but not to win.

Netanyahu's right-wing bloc is down from last elections performance but has denied the opposition a decisive majority. The election that was supposed to be a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership after the catastrophic security failures of October 7, 2023 ended in a virtual tie. Neither bloc can muster the 61 seats needed to govern. The country is split down the middle, and the fundamental question of who should lead it remains unanswered.

Netanyahu's Likud remains the largest single party with around 25 seats, but the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party is close behind with 23-24 seats. When grouped into blocs, the picture is even starker: Netanyahu's right-wing and religious parties command approximately 53 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu opposition holds roughly 48. Neither side comes close to the 61-seat threshold.

The high turnout, nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, reflected intense public engagement and a genuine desire for change. Yet the result showed a nation politically split down the middle, unable or unwilling to deliver a decisive verdict on its longest-serving leader.

What makes this impasse even more remarkable is the position of the Arab parties, which are projected to win a record 18-19 seats. Suddenly, they find themselves in a potential kingmaker role, even though both major blocs had ruled out including them in a coalition. This is the paradox of Israeli politics: the Arab minority can influence the outcome but cannot participate in governance. Their electoral strength is real, but their political power remains illusory.

Netanyahu knows he has not won. He has survived, barely, and he knows that his survival depends on forces beyond his control. Facing an ICC arrest warrant and domestic corruption charges, he has immense personal incentive to cling to power. He also hinted at a potential regional escalation involving Iran, a move that could shift the political dynamic or delay coalition talks. This is not statesmanship; it is survival tactics dressed up as leadership.

Eisenkot ran a campaign centered on accountability and integrity. His personal story, a bereaved father whose son fell in Gaza, a Mizrahi Jew from a demographic that typically leans right, gave him a unique appeal.

Eisenkot's allegations during the campaign were specific and damning. He accused Netanyahu of using national security for political survival, citing the prime minister's posting of AI-generated images of a nuclear bomb over Tel Aviv on election eve as "hysterical" fearmongering. He blamed Netanyahu of trying to sabotage the electoral process by attempting to meet with the police commissioner on election eve to discuss so-called election integrity issues. He targeted Netanyahu of failing to achieve the stated war objectives, pointing out that the promise of "total victory" had yielded nothing but a shift from "total victory" to "not surrendering".

These are not minor disagreements. They are fundamental indictments of a leader who, according to his challenger, has put his personal survival above the national interest.

Eisenkot's path to the premiership is mathematically possible but politically fraught. To become prime minister, he would need 61 seats. With his bloc at roughly 51-53 seats, he would need the outside support or inclusion of the Arab parties. But Eisenkot had explicitly ruled out governing with Arab parties during the campaign, and Netanyahu was already using this as a scare tactic, claiming such a government would lack legitimacy.

This leaves Eisenkot with two options, both deeply problematic. He could attempt a narrow minority government relying on Arab parties to abstain from key votes, a fragile arrangement that could collapse at any moment. Or he could form a unity government with Likud, a national emergency government that many in the opposition reject but which might be forced by the stalemate.

Both options are bad. The first is unstable and vulnerable to Netanyahu's scare tactics. The second requires Eisenkot to govern alongside the man he has accused of sabotaging democracy and failing the nation. Neither represents the change that the electorate apparently wanted.

Other two options are equally unstable, continuing with the stalemate leading to another election or Netanyahu trying to break Eisenkot allies to form another lose government.

Amid all the horse-race analysis and coalition arithmetic, a deeper truth is being overlooked. The strong showing of Arab-majority parties does not signal a fundamental shift in Israel's political direction or its approach to the Palestinians. This is a caution against overreading the election results. Even if Arab-led parties win more seats, the structural and ideological makeup of Israeli politics, particularly the dominance of right-wing and security-focused blocs remains intact. Those who see in these results evidence of a moderating or transforming Israel are engaging in wishful thinking. The election confirmed that the country remains evenly divided between those who want Netanyahu gone and those who still trust him to manage the country's security. It did not resolve the fundamental question of Israel's leadership. It merely confirmed that the country is stuck.

With final results due on November 4, the nation faces weeks of intense bargaining. Netanyahu, facing legal peril and political isolation, has every incentive to cling to power and to escalate regional tensions if it serves his interests. Eisenkot has warned him not to use security for political ends, stating: "Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs." But warnings are not constraints.

The election did not resolve Israel's leadership crisis. It did not deliver a verdict on October 7. It did not produce a government. It produced a stalemate, and stalemates in Israeli politics tend to favour the incumbent, especially one as skilled at survival as Netanyahu.

So, what's the final verdict. Not a victory. Not a change. Just a deadlock, and a nation waiting to see what happens next.

headline: Justice lost in indices
description: Justice lost in indices
author: Dr Shahid Hussain Kamboyo
article_text:
International rankings influence public opinion, but their meaning can be distorted when numbers are detached from what they measure. Pakistan's position in the World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index 2025 has often been presented as a verdict on the judiciary. The concern is understandable, but the interpretation is incomplete. A national assessment covering institutions cannot fairly become the scorecard of one. Accountability begins with identifying who is responsible for what.

Pakistan ranked 130th among 143 countries, scoring 0.37. The Index examines eight dimensions, including constraints on government powers, corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Courts influence several of these dimensions, but do not determine them all. Pakistan stood last in Order and Security, a measure principally concerned with public safety. A country's overall standing must therefore be read as a picture of its wider rule-of-law environment, not an exclusive judgment on its courts.

Comparisons reinforce the distinction. Pakistan ranked 129th in Civil Justice and 101st in Criminal Justice. Bangladesh, although ranked 125th overall, stood 132nd and 118th in these categories. Türkiye ranked 118th overall but 106th in Criminal Justice; the Russian Federation stood 119th overall but 128th in that category. Brazil, despite ranking 78th overall, stood 111th in Criminal Justice. These figures establish no superiority of Pakistan's judiciary. They simply show that an overall ranking and its individual components tell different stories. Statistics are useful only when the conclusions drawn from them remain faithful to their meaning.

The World Bank's World Development Report 2017: Governance and the Law underscores the importance of institutional cooperation and effective implementation. Investigation, prosecution, adjudication and enforcement form different parts of the justice process. Their responsibilities intersect, but they are not interchangeable. Fair criticism should illuminate these connections rather than obscure them.

Yet the WJP scorecard also identifies weaknesses that cannot be explained away. Pakistan scored 0.36 on accessibility and affordability of civil justice, 0.28 on unreasonable delay and 0.35 on effective enforcement. For people seeking justice, these are not abstract deficiencies. A court visit may cost a labourer a day's wages. A lawyer's fee may compete with school expenses or medicines. A widow pursuing inheritance may struggle simply to understand where to begin. A right guaranteed by law has limited meaning if the person entitled to it cannot afford to claim it. Justice must therefore become accessible beyond the formal promise of an open courtroom.

This is why the Supreme Court's Journey Through Reform & Innovation 2026 deserves attention. Its 86-point agenda, pursued since November 2024, addresses barriers of cost, distance, information and delay. The September 2026 reform matrix records 64 completed actions, with others still requiring implementation. Such progress offers grounds for hope, but a completed administrative task is not necessarily a transformed public experience. Reform earns confidence when its benefits reach the people for whom it was designed.

The Public Facilitation Centre provides a clearer point of contact for court-related information and assistance. Digital processing of certified copies and video-link facilities can spare litigants unnecessary journeys, while advanced electronic filing remains under development. The Overseas Litigants' Facilitation Cell assists those separated from proceedings by distance. Free legal advice arrangements and improvements in women-centred facilities, alongside plans for dedicated Women Facilitation Centres, seek to reduce barriers faced by vulnerable court users. These are practical responses to the WJP's concerns about accessibility and affordability. Their promise lies in bringing judicial services closer to citizens, rather than leaving citizens to navigate every obstacle alone.

Delay demands equal attention. The Supreme Court recorded approximately 56 per cent more case disposals in 202425 than in 202324, while performance remained substantially above the earlier level in 202526. District courts decided approximately 1.47 million time-bound cases between September 2025 and July 2026. Better case management, prioritised hearings and monitoring indicate sustained efforts, although disposal totals cannot by themselves prove that waiting times have fallen for everyone. A judgment delivered after years of hardship may vindicate a right without restoring what delay has taken. Judicial efficiency must ultimately be measured in time saved for litigants, not numbers alone.

Enforcement presents another challenge. A favourable civil judgment means little if its remedy remains beyond reach. Criminal justice likewise depends upon credible investigation, effective prosecution, fair trials and lawful correctional processes. Each institution must discharge its own duties, while cooperation ensures that a legal decision becomes practical relief. The rule of law is strengthened when responsibility is shared appropriately, not when accountability is shifted elsewhere.

International indices can reveal shortcomings and encourage reform, but surveys and expert assessments should be considered alongside institutional records and lived experience. Some evidence underlying annual assessments predates recent changes, whose effects may take time to emerge. Pakistan's ranking warrants reflection, neither dismissal nor indiscriminate blame. Ultimately, justice must be felt in the worker who recovers his wages, the widow who secures her inheritance, and the pensioner who receives relief while it still matters. The true measure of progress is not a better place on a table, but a lasting public confidence that the law will protect people when they need it most.

International rankings influence public opinion, but their meaning can be distorted when numbers are detached from what they measure. Pakistan's position in the World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index 2025 has often been presented as a verdict on the judiciary. The concern is understandable, but the interpretation is incomplete. A national assessment covering institutions cannot fairly become the scorecard of one. Accountability begins with identifying who is responsible for what.

Pakistan ranked 130th among 143 countries, scoring 0.37. The Index examines eight dimensions, including constraints on government powers, corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Courts influence several of these dimensions, but do not determine them all. Pakistan stood last in Order and Security, a measure principally concerned with public safety. A country's overall standing must therefore be read as a picture of its wider rule-of-law environment, not an exclusive judgment on its courts.

Comparisons reinforce the distinction. Pakistan ranked 129th in Civil Justice and 101st in Criminal Justice. Bangladesh, although ranked 125th overall, stood 132nd and 118th in these categories. Türkiye ranked 118th overall but 106th in Criminal Justice; the Russian Federation stood 119th overall but 128th in that category. Brazil, despite ranking 78th overall, stood 111th in Criminal Justice. These figures establish no superiority of Pakistan's judiciary. They simply show that an overall ranking and its individual components tell different stories. Statistics are useful only when the conclusions drawn from them remain faithful to their meaning.

The World Bank's World Development Report 2017: Governance and the Law underscores the importance of institutional cooperation and effective implementation. Investigation, prosecution, adjudication and enforcement form different parts of the justice process. Their responsibilities intersect, but they are not interchangeable. Fair criticism should illuminate these connections rather than obscure them.

Yet the WJP scorecard also identifies weaknesses that cannot be explained away. Pakistan scored 0.36 on accessibility and affordability of civil justice, 0.28 on unreasonable delay and 0.35 on effective enforcement. For people seeking justice, these are not abstract deficiencies. A court visit may cost a labourer a day's wages. A lawyer's fee may compete with school expenses or medicines. Justice must therefore become accessible beyond the formal promise of an open courtroom.

Its 86-point agenda, pursued since November 2024, addresses barriers of cost, distance, information and delay. The September 2026 reform matrix records 64 completed actions, with others still requiring implementation. Reform earns confidence when its benefits reach the people for whom it was designed.

Digital processing of certified copies and video-link facilities can spare litigants unnecessary journeys, while advanced electronic filing remains under development. headline: Real problem is execution, not ideas
description: Real problem is execution, not ideas
author: DR MANZOOR AHMAD
article_text:
The recent conference on Pakistan at Harvard University, themed "From Potential to Performance", has generated considerable debate in Pakistan, partly because of the deep pessimism expressed by two highly acclaimed economists about the country's economic performance compared with its peers.

One of the panellists, Nobel laureate Professor Acemoglu, described Pakistan's economy as having been "comatose" for the past three decades. He attributed this to weak institutions, inadequate investment in education and low tax collection. Unless these serious political economy failures are recognised and addressed, reversing the downward trajectory will be extremely difficult. With the world now being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI), he warned that Pakistan appears largely unprepared, lacking the digital infrastructure needed to keep pace and risking further marginalisation.

Another panellist, Professor Atif Mian, argued that Pakistan lacked the strategic vision needed to tackle fundamental problems, including elite capture, the failure to achieve inclusive growth and insufficient efforts to establish peace within the country. He particularly noted that although Pakistan could address its energy crisis by electrifying its transport sector, it had been unable to do so because it could not confront powerful pressure groups.

Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb, who also participated in the panel, acknowledged that these challenges were well understood but argued that political economy constraints had repeatedly delayed difficult decisions and their implementation. However, he maintained that the situation was changing for the better, as decisions previously postponed were now being taken and implemented. In particular, he cited long-stalled tariff reforms, the taxation of agricultural income by provincial governments and the privatisation of state-owned enterprises.

The question is whether these developments represent a genuine shift in Pakistan's political economy, with reforms overcoming resistance from powerful interest groups, or whether the country remains on the downward trajectory described by the two economists. Let us first examine three areas where reforms have been blocked for decades.

The first is the powerful industrial lobby, which has long feared that opening the economy before addressing fundamental issues such as energy costs, interest rates, taxation, and law and order could seriously damage domestic manufacturing. With the launch of the five-year National Tariff Policy, the government has indeed embarked on a radical programme of trade liberalisation and making the industry competitive. The reforms are now in their second year of implementation and, with the notable exception of the automotive sector, have faced less resistance from other industrial sectors than many had anticipated. Furthermore, the predicted collapse of domestic industry and a big fall in import-related revenue have not materialised, while several indicators point towards a more positive outcome.

The second major lobby comprises those opposing the expansion of the tax net to previously undertaxed sectors, particularly agricultural income and the retail and wholesale sectors. Here, the picture is mixed. Although provincial governments have enacted legislation to tax agricultural income, it remains unclear whether these measures will deliver the intended results. The government's experience with the retail sector shows that legislation and concessions alone cannot achieve the desired outcomes without the political will to confront resistance from powerful interest groups. Nevertheless, after remaining below 10% for almost a decade, the tax-to-GDP ratio rose from 8.8% in FY2024 to 10.3% in FY2025. This 1.5-percentage-point increase is a significant achievement.

Another major source of resistance has been trade unions and organised labour, which have opposed the privatisation of state-owned enterprises for decades. However, the government has begun to break this longstanding stalemate through the sale of Pakistan International Airlines and the closure of Utility Stores Corporation. It is now proceeding with a broader programme involving 27 state-owned enterprises. Whether this momentum can be sustained remains to be seen, but the willingness to take decisions previously considered politically difficult is an encouraging development.

Regarding Professor Acemoglu's assertion that Pakistan is poorly prepared for the AI revolution, the finance minister has rightly pointed out that the country has already taken important steps in this direction. Pakistan approved its National AI Policy in 2025, while its IT exports have reached $4.6 billion and are growing at around 20% annually. The government plans to upskill its IT workforce, already the world's third largest in terms of outsourcing talent, and invest $1 billion in AI by 2030. The World Bank also recognises Pakistan as one of the leading hosts of data centres in the MENAP region, alongside Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Its initiatives in blockchain technology and the regulation of digital assets, including cryptocurrencies, further demonstrate that Pakistan is beginning to position itself to benefit from emerging technologies.

As for Professor Mian's observation that Pakistan has failed to make full use of its solar potential, it is true that the country has moved relatively slowly towards the electrification of transport, partly because powerful automobile lobbies have sought to slow the transition. However, the picture is quite different when it comes to solar energy. Pakistan has emerged as one of the more successful developing countries in adopting solar power, with installed solar capacity estimated at around 8,000 MW. It is now among the countries where renewable energy has overtaken fossil fuels in electricity generation.

The overall picture is mixed, but there are reasons for cautious optimism. Recent initiatives in tariff liberalisation, taxation, privatisation, solar energy, digitalisation and AI suggest that Pakistan may finally be beginning to turn a corner. But after decades of economic underperformance, incremental change will not be enough. The pace of reform must accelerate, and difficult decisions must no longer be postponed to accommodate entrenched interests.

The real test is whether these reforms can be implemented consistently, withstand political and institutional resistance, and translate into higher productivity, greater investment, stronger exports and sustained economic growth. Pakistan does not suffer from a shortage of ideas, diagnoses or policy prescriptions. Its real challenge is to overcome the resistance to change and turn sound policies into action. The time for promises and plans is over; what Pakistan needs now is execution.

The writer is a Senior Fellow at PIDE and has previously served as Pakistan's ambassador and permanent representative to the World Trade Organisation

ISLAMABAD:

The recent conference on Pakistan at Harvard University, themed "From Potential to Performance", has generated considerable debate in Pakistan, partly because of the deep pessimism expressed by two highly acclaimed economists about the country's economic performance compared with its peers.

One of the panellists, Nobel laureate Professor Acemoglu, described Pakistan's economy as having been "comatose" for the past three decades. He attributed this to weak institutions, inadequate investment in education and low tax collection. Unless these serious political economy failures are recognised and addressed, reversing the downward trajectory will be extremely difficult. With the world now being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI), he warned that Pakistan appears largely unprepared, lacking the digital infrastructure needed to keep pace and risking further marginalisation.

Another panellist, Professor Atif Mian, argued that Pakistan lacked the strategic vision needed to tackle fundamental problems, including elite capture, the failure to achieve inclusive growth and insufficient efforts to establish peace within the country. He particularly noted that although Pakistan could address its energy crisis by electrifying its transport sector, it had been unable to do so because it could not confront powerful pressure groups.

Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb, who also participated in the panel, acknowledged that these challenges were well understood but argued that political economy constraints had repeatedly delayed difficult decisions and their implementation. However, he maintained that the situation was changing for the better, as decisions previously postponed were now being taken and implemented. In particular, he cited long-stalled tariff reforms, the taxation of agricultural income by provincial governments and the privatisation of state-owned enterprises.

The question is whether these developments represent a genuine shift in Pakistan's political economy, with reforms overcoming resistance from powerful interest groups, or whether the country remains on the downward trajectory described by the two economists. Let us first examine three areas where reforms have been blocked for decades.

The first is the powerful industrial lobby, which has long feared that opening the economy before addressing fundamental issues such as energy costs, interest rates, taxation, and law and order could seriously damage domestic manufacturing. With the launch of the five-year National Tariff Policy, the government has indeed embarked on a radical programme of trade liberalisation and making the industry competitive. The reforms are now in their second year of implementation and, with the notable exception of the automotive sector, have faced less resistance from other industrial sectors than many had anticipated. Furthermore, the predicted collapse of domestic industry and a big fall in import-related revenue have not materialised, while several indicators point towards a more positive outcome.

The second major lobby comprises those opposing the expansion of the tax net to previously undertaxed sectors, particularly agricultural income and the retail and wholesale sectors. Here, the picture is mixed. Although provincial governments have enacted legislation to tax agricultural income, it remains unclear whether these measures will deliver the intended results. The government's experience with the retail sector shows that legislation and concessions alone cannot achieve the desired outcomes without the political will to confront resistance from powerful interest groups. Nevertheless, after remaining below 10% for almost a decade, the tax-to-GDP ratio rose from 8.8% in FY2024 to 10.3% in FY2025. This 1.5-percentage-point increase is a significant achievement.

Another major source of resistance has been trade unions and organised labour, which have opposed the privatisation of state-owned enterprises for decades. However, the government has begun to break this longstanding stalemate through the sale of Pakistan International Airlines and the closure of Utility Stores Corporation. It is now proceeding with a broader programme involving 27 state-owned enterprises. Whether this momentum can be sustained remains to be seen, but the willingness to take decisions previously considered politically difficult is an encouraging development.

Regarding Professor Acemoglu's assertion that Pakistan is poorly prepared for the AI revolution, the finance minister has rightly pointed out that the country has already taken important steps in this direction. Pakistan approved its National AI Policy in 2025, while its IT exports have reached $4.6 billion and are growing at around 20% annually. The government plans to upskill its IT workforce, already the world's third largest in terms of outsourcing talent, and invest $1 billion in AI by 2030. The World Bank also recognises Pakistan as one of the leading hosts of data centres in the MENAP region, alongside Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Its initiatives in blockchain technology and the regulation of digital assets, including cryptocurrencies, further demonstrate that Pakistan is beginning to position itself to benefit from emerging technologies.

As for Professor Mian's observation that Pakistan has failed to make full use of its solar potential, it is true that the country has moved relatively slowly towards the electrification of transport, partly because powerful automobile lobbies have sought to slow the transition. However, the picture is quite different when it comes to solar energy. Pakistan has emerged as one of the more successful developing countries in adopting solar power, with installed solar capacity estimated at around 8,000 MW. It is now among the countries where renewable energy has overtaken fossil fuels in electricity generation.

The overall picture is mixed, but there are reasons for cautious optimism. Recent initiatives in tariff liberalisation, taxation, privatisation, solar energy, digitalisation and AI suggest that Pakistan may finally be beginning to turn a corner. But after decades of economic underperformance, incremental change will not be enough. The pace of reform must accelerate, and difficult decisions must no longer be postponed to accommodate entrenched interests.

The real test is whether these reforms can be implemented consistently, withstand political and institutional resistance, and translate into higher productivity, greater investment, stronger exports and sustained economic growth. Pakistan does not suffer from a shortage of ideas, diagnoses or policy prescriptions. Its real challenge is to overcome the resistance to change and turn sound policies into action. The time for promises and plans is over; what Pakistan needs now is execution.

headline: New provinces will cost more than they deliver
description: New provinces will cost more than they deliver
author: Maryam Ayub
article_text:
In Pakistan's policy and political circles, the debate over the creation of new provinces has resurfaced again with unusual intensity. Different proposals are coming not only from regional political movements, but also from senior government officials, universities and policy institutions.

The case for creating additional provinces is increasingly linked to persistent regional disparities in socio-economic indicators, particularly where low-performing areas remain geographically distant from the provincial capitals and centres of decision-making. These persistent disparities are often associated with structural imbalances arising from the concentration of large and demographically diverse populations within geographically broad administrative units. Poverty rates also vary significantly across provinces, that is Punjab at 23.3%, Sindh at 32.6%, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa at 35.3% and Balochistan at 47%. Such differences highlight the uneven socio-economic conditions that persist under the current provincial structure.

Advocates of provincial restructuring further argue that creation of additional provinces would improve governance, public service delivery and citizen welfare by bringing decision-making closer to underserved regions. The size and administrative complexity of the existing provinces are viewed as contributing to disparities in access to public service delivery.

Our recent report, on the contrary, suggests that reorganisation of the federation into many smaller provinces, while remaining within the existing resource envelope, will most likely deteriorate the quality of public service delivery, particularly in provinces with smaller population size. The fiscal case for creation of new provinces remains weak, and in fact missing. Therefore, any attempt to increase the number of provinces will increase fiscal stress for Pakistan, which we can ill-afford especially as we are now in the last year of the IMF programme.

The report considers two restructuring scenarios. Scenario A divides Punjab into Bahawalpur, South Punjab and the remaining Punjab, increasing the number of provinces from four to six. Scenario B treats each existing administrative division within Punjab, Sindh, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan as a province, resulting in 30 provinces.

The NFC exercise uses a nested allocation approach in which each existing province retains its current 7th NFC share, which is then distributed among its successor units according to the existing NFC criteria of population, poverty and backwardness, revenue collection or generation and inverse population density. Under Scenario A, South Punjab receives an illustrative allocation of Rs1,001.06 billion, while Bahawalpur receives Rs537.01 billion. Under Scenario B, allocations differ considerably, ranging from Rs720.94 billion for Lahore and Rs690.84 billion for Karachi to Rs45.62 billion for Loralai and Rs49.83 billion for Zhob. Eleven of the 30 proposed units receive less than Rs150 billion.

The most important finding emerges when these fixed institutional costs are compared with the NFC resources available to individual proposed provinces. Large units such as Lahore and Karachi would spend only around 3% to 4% of their illustrative NFC allocations on the core provincial structure, while the burden rises sharply for smaller units.

Using a 10% fiscal sustainability benchmark based on the low recurring-cost estimate, 16 of the 30 proposed provinces under Scenario B remain at or below the threshold, while 14 exceed it. The burden is particularly high in the smallest units. The core provincial structure would absorb around 49% of Loralai's allocation, 45% of Zhob's and 37% of Rakhshan's even under the low-cost estimate.

A provincial government requires a minimum political, administrative and judicial structure irrespective of population size. Consequently, these costs represent only a small share of the resources available to large proposed provinces but absorb a much greater proportion of the NFC allocation of smaller units. Every proposed province with a population below 1.2 million would require more than one-third of its illustrative NFC allocation to finance the core provincial government structure. The findings therefore show that the fiscal implications of restructuring depend strongly on the number and size of the provinces created. Limited restructuring involving relatively large units produces a much smaller recurring burden, whereas several smaller division-based provinces would face disproportionately high administrative costs relative to their expected NFC resources.

This pressure would be higher for proposed provinces with relatively small NFC allocations and limited revenue generation capacity. Where a larger share of available resources is absorbed by the recurring cost of provincial institutions, less fiscal space would remain for other provincial expenditures, including education, health, infrastructure and development spending. Smaller and fiscally weaker provinces would therefore face a greater risk that institutional costs crowd out resources available for public service delivery.

The proposed restructuring would also generate some additional expenditure at the federal level, particularly through changes in Senate representation, but the larger fiscal pressure would arise at the provincial level. Any proposal for new provinces should therefore be accompanied by a formal fiscal costing exercise, consideration of the resource base of the proposed units and application of a fiscal screening benchmark to assess whether recurring provincial-government costs remain proportionate to available resources.

Where the primary objective is improved access to government and public services, stronger local governments should be considered as an alternative to replicating the full structure of provincial government. That itself needs serious research on constitutional arrangements, political economy and institutional implications.

THE WRITERS ARE AFFILIATED WITH PRIME INSTITUTE, AN INDEPENDENT ECONOMIC POLICY THINK TANK

The most important finding emerges when these fixed institutional costs are compared with the NFC resources available to individual proposed provinces. Large units such as Lahore and Karachi would spend only around 3% to 4% of their illustrative NFC allocations on the core provincial structure, while the burden rises sharply for smaller units.

The findings therefore show that the fiscal implications of restructuring depend strongly on the number and size of the provinces created. Limited restructuring involving relatively large units produces a much smaller recurring burden, whereas several smaller division-based provinces would face disproportionately high administrative costs relative to their expected NFC resources.

This pressure would be higher for proposed provinces with relatively small NFC allocations and limited revenue generation capacity. Where a larger share of available resources is absorbed by the recurring cost of provincial institutions, less fiscal space would remain for other provincial expenditures, including education, health, infrastructure and development spending. Smaller and fiscally weaker provinces would therefore face a greater risk that institutional costs crowd out resources available for public service delivery.

The proposed restructuring would also generate some additional expenditure at the federal level, particularly through changes in Senate representation, but the larger fiscal pressure would arise at the provincial level. Any proposal for new provinces should therefore be accompanied by a formal fiscal costing exercise, consideration of the resource base of the proposed units and application of a fiscal screening benchmark to assess whether recurring provincial-government costs remain proportionate to available resources.

Where the primary objective is improved access to government and public services, stronger local governments should be considered as an alternative to replicating the full structure of provincial government. That itself needs serious research on constitutional arrangements, political economy and institutional implications.

headline: The AI accord leaves weapons out
description: The AI accord leaves weapons out
author: Faran Mahmood
article_text:
Last month MI5 Director General, Sir Ken McCallum, announced the launch of the Threat Assessmnent Center (AITAC) during his annual national security threat update at Thames House in London.

Talking about "polarising algorithms" Sir Ken McCallum pointed out how AI was supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders.

This warning from intelligence officials coincided with an unprecedented shift in September 2026, when heads of leading AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI, called for slowing the pace of frontier development. Three developments drove the shift. In one incident, AI agents hacked Hugging Face and OpenAI's systems and effectively slipped out of containment. There was evidence of attempts to use Claude for bioweapons research. And public anxiety built steadily.

Despite these warnings, everyone remains locked in a classic prisoner's dilemma. No single entity wants to slow down unilaterally, given the massive capital expenditure flowing into chip exports. The pressure is both financial and competitive, particularly as leading frontier labs head towards public offerings.

Anthropic's leaked IPO filing showed a 2025 operating loss of $8 billion, and other frontier labs are in the same position. At the same time, China's AI stocks are down 40% since June, with over $480 billion of wealth gone. Stocks are rushing to enter IPO as the STAR50 plunges into bear territory, and founders are trying to cash out. At the same time, this commercial arms race is matched at the nation-state level, where both the United States and China treat AI leadership as existential.

While Washington and Beijing dominate the frontier, the battlefield in Eastern Europe illustrates the physical reality of this race. Russia lags as much as four years behind the United States and China, and recent attacks by Ukrainian drones on three Yandex data centres powered by Nvidia A100 chips have caused considerable damage to its AI programme. The irony here is that the drones which hit the AI infrastructure were themselves AI-powered autonomous weapons.

This brings us to a bigger question. How should AI technologies be regulated in general, and autonomous weapons in particular, which now include cyber agents and kinetic drones? The White House Accord on Super Intelligence (SI), signed on September 29, fails to answer this question. It proposes internal safety controls, an oversight team and external audits that ensure continuous monitoring of models during training and deployment to prevent risks in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

However, it does not regulate the wider landscape of autonomous weapons or rogue AI agents capable of initiating sophisticated cyber-attacks. It does not address risks from the air, such as autonomous or AI-powered drones, whether from acts of war or from terrorism. Nor is there anything in the White House Accord on SI that legally compels signatories to take appropriate measures. Without structural changes to commercial incentives, the accord risks acting as little more than a convenient cover for labs seeking to curb loss-making capital expenditure.

Now US policy hawks are looking for a similar accord on AI with China related to AI safety and controls, perhaps modelled on Cold War arms control negotiations. At present, China's own production of AI compute is only around 4% of that of the United States, and the majority of China's computing power comes from smuggled and remotely accessed US chips. By some estimates, US AI labs are somewhere between six and twelve months ahead of the Chinese, and US policymakers believe the United States needs to extend this lead by up to two years before negotiating an AI agreement with China. They believe that closing loopholes in export controls would expand the US lead in AI, and could force China to conclude that cutting a deal soon would be preferable to an even more lopsided deal later.

This dynamic highlights a fundamental historical hurdle. Past arms control treaties succeeded because they regulated power between equals. Every past bilateral strategic arms control agreement was either negotiated between countries that were already at overall strategic parity, or agreed only after one country concluded that it was better to lock itself into a disadvantageous position because it could not win the strategic competition.

Historically, there is no example in which two states of unequal strength concluded an agreement to regulate a strategically critical technology that either caused the leader to give up its overall strategic advantage or constrained the other state's development capabilities. For example, the SALT II, START and New START (2010) agreements capped nuclear warheads for both countries at identical levels. The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty did the same by putting similar caps on the deployment of missile defence systems.

This does not mean an AI arms control pact is totally out of the question. Beijing is genuinely concerned about AI, and China's top spy chief has warned that it poses a serious threat to the Chinese Communist Party's rule and overall political stability. The recent market turbulence indicates that CoP-style deliberations are still possible, if both superpowers remain sincere about mitigating existential security risks and preventing an unregulated race towards autonomous warfare.

THE WRITER IS A CAMBRIDGE GRADUATE AND WORKS AS A STRATEGY CONSULTANT
