This brings us to a bigger question. How should AI technologies be regulated in general, and autonomous weapons in particular, which now include cyber agents and kinetic drones? The White House Accord on Super Intelligence (SI), signed on September 29, fails to answer this question. It proposes internal safety controls, an oversight team and external audits that ensure continuous monitoring of models during training and deployment to prevent risks in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

However, it does not regulate the wider landscape of autonomous weapons or rogue AI agents capable of initiating sophisticated cyber-attacks. It does not address risks from the air, such as autonomous or AI-powered drones, whether from acts of war or from terrorism. Nor is there anything in the White House Accord on SI that legally compels signatories to take appropriate measures. Without structural changes to commercial incentives, the accord risks acting as little more than a convenient cover for labs seeking to curb loss-making capital expenditure.

Now US policy hawks are looking for a similar accord on AI with China related to AI safety and controls, perhaps modelled on Cold War arms control negotiations. At present, China's own production of AI compute is only around 4% of that of the United States, and the majority of China's computing power comes from smuggled and remotely accessed US chips. By some estimates, US AI labs are somewhere between six and twelve months ahead of the Chinese, and US policymakers believe the United States needs to extend this lead by up to two years before negotiating an AI agreement with China. They believe that closing loopholes in export controls would expand the US lead in AI, and could force China to conclude that cutting a deal soon would be preferable to an even more lopsided deal later.

This dynamic highlights a fundamental historical hurdle. Past arms control treaties succeeded because they regulated power between equals. Every past bilateral strategic arms control agreement was either negotiated between countries that were already at overall strategic parity, or agreed only after one country concluded that it was better to lock itself into a disadvantageous position because it could not win the strategic competition.

Historically, there is no example in which two states of unequal strength concluded an agreement to regulate a strategically critical technology that either caused the leader to give up its overall strategic advantage or constrained the other state's development capabilities. For example, the SALT II, START and New START (2010) agreements capped nuclear warheads for both countries at identical levels. The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty did the same by putting similar caps on the deployment of missile defence systems.

This does not mean an AI arms control pact is totally out of the question. Beijing is genuinely concerned about AI, and China's top spy chief has warned that it poses a serious threat to the Chinese Communist Party's rule and overall political stability. The recent market turbulence indicates that CoP-style deliberations are still possible, if both superpowers remain sincere about mitigating existential security risks and preventing an unregulated race towards autonomous warfare.

headline: Stubble: an opportunity to earn
description: Stubble: an opportunity to earn
author: SHAMSUL ISLAM KHAN
article_text:
Every year, as winter approaches, Lahore and other cities across Punjab are engulfed by hazardous smog, posing serious risks to public health, disrupting daily life and reducing visibility. Environmental experts frequently identify crop-residue burning, particularly rice-stubble burning in Punjab and across the border in India, as a major contributor to seasonal air pollution.

However, smog also results from vehicle emissions, industrial smoke, brick kilns, construction dust and other pollutants. Weather conditions, including low wind speeds and temperature inversions, further trap pollutants close to the ground. Addressing this recurring crisis requires scientific assessment of pollution sources, stricter emissions controls, cleaner agricultural practices and coordinated regional action.

Pakistan's smog problem also exposes a wider economic failure: agricultural waste that could generate income is often treated as a nuisance. According to a UNDP report on rural revitalisation in China, more than 647 million tonnes of crop straw were recycled in 2021, achieving a utilisation rate of nearly 90%. This demonstrates the potential of converting agricultural residues into valuable economic resources.

Rice straw can be used for animal feed, bio-fertilisers, industrial raw materials and mushroom cultivation. Rice bran can be used for bran edible oil, husk can support biomass co-generation energy, ash, silica, blocks and other industrial applications. Research and investment can also explore rice straw-based boards, packaging materials, yarn and other products.

In Pakistan, however, rice straw is frequently burnt in fields, husk accumulates at rice mills, and valuable byproducts remain underutilised. At a time when the country urgently needs higher exports, rural employment, affordable energy and import substitution, this represents a substantial missed opportunity.

Beyond subsidies and penalties

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has launched a subsidy under the Punjab Clean Air Programme, offering rice growers Rs5,000 per acre, subject to a maximum of Rs25,000 per farmer, to discourage stubble burning. The initiative provides immediate assistance, but financial incentives alone cannot establish a permanent solution. Similarly, imposing fines on farmers and FIRs without providing practical and economically viable alternatives are unlikely to eliminate the problem sustainably. Pakistan needs to transform stubble management from a pollution-control exercise into a commercially viable agricultural industry.

Waste-to-Wealth Company

The Punjab government should establish an Agricultural Waste-to-Wealth Company to develop an integrated system for collecting, processing and marketing agricultural residues, beginning with rice straw and husk. Its principal responsibilities should include:

1-Rice-straw collection network: Establish collection centres in major rice-producing districts and provide balers, shredders and transportation through cooperatives and private contractors. Farmers should receive commercially viable prices for usable straw, creating a financial incentive to stop burning it. Collection operations must be organised around the short interval between rice harvesting and the planting of the next crop. Timely removal is essential if farmers are to adopt alternative practices.

2-Industrial utilisation and value addition: Encourage rice mills to utilise paddy husk for biomass power generation and industrial heat where economically feasible. Develop composting and organic-fertiliser facilities, and promote rice straw-based boards, packaging materials and other suitable manufactured products. Research institutions and businesses should investigate advanced applications, including biofuels and cellulose-based products. Where technically and commercially viable, cellulose extracted from rice straw could provide raw material for industrial applications, potentially including textile fibres and yarn. The objective should be to develop multiple uses for agricultural residues rather than depend on a single technology or market.

3-Private-sector investment: Invite domestic and foreign investors' joint ventures to establish agricultural waste processing facilities in rice-producing regions. The government should offer transparent, time-bound incentives linked to actual production, investment and verified residue utilisation. Long-term supply agreements between farmers, collection companies, rice mills and industrial consumers would help establish reliable supply chains and reduce commercial uncertainty.

4-Farmer participation and mechanisation: Farmers must be partners in the proposed system, not merely the targets of enforcement. Machinery for chopping, collecting, baling and transporting straw should be made accessible through service providers, cooperatives and affordable financing. Financial institutions, including Zarai Taraqiati Bank Limited and Apna Kissan Bank, could support eligible investments in agricultural machinery, collection centres, storage facilities and residue-processing projects. The government should aid coordination among agricultural departments, rice mills, research institutions and trade associations to ensure that collection and processing systems operate efficiently.

From agricultural waste to economic value

An integrated waste-to-wealth system could deliver several benefits simultaneously. These include reducing open-field burning and helping mitigate seasonal air pollution, generating additional income for rice farmers, creating rural employment and new businesses, supplying raw materials to energy and manufacturing industries, encouraging investment in agricultural technology, reducing waste and supporting import substitution, and developing new products with potential for domestic sales and exports.

However, success will depend on suitable technology, transport costs, reliable buyers and the economics of individual applications. Not all rice straw can be collected or processed profitably. Local feasibility studies and pilot projects should therefore precede large-scale investment. Punjab and Sindh should adapt their approaches to local agricultural conditions, infrastructure and industrial demand. The objective should be to establish commercially sustainable systems rather than create permanent dependence on subsidies.

Role of trade associations

Trade associations also have a responsibility beyond lobbying for their members' immediate demands. They should help develop the research, technology and industrial capabilities needed to make entire sectors more competitive. Pakistan's rice industry offers an opportunity to build clusters around agricultural residues, including straw, husk, bran and other byproducts. Such industries could diversify revenue streams, strengthen rural economies and improve the sector's overall competitiveness. After 79 years of independence, Pakistan needs less ceremonial and more economic leadership: laboratories instead of excessive ceremony, technology instead of trophy sales, and measurable results instead of publicity.

Stubble management must evolve from a policy focused primarily on controlling burning into a comprehensive resource-recovery industry. The government should facilitate investment, establish collection infrastructure, support research and create a regulatory environment in which agricultural waste becomes a commercially valuable resource. Farmers should earn from residues that currently impose disposal costs, while businesses should have incentives to convert them into marketable products. Pakistan's next rice revolution should not be measured solely by how much rice the country grows or exports, but by how much additional value it creates from every ton, and how little it wastes.

The writer is a former vice president of Karachi Chamber of Commerce & Industry and former board member of REAP

According to a UNDP report on rural revitalisation in China, more than 647 million tonnes of crop straw were recycled in 2021, achieving a utilisation rate of nearly 90%. This demonstrates the potential of converting agricultural residues into valuable economic resources.

Rice straw can be used for animal feed, bio-fertilisers, industrial raw materials and mushroom cultivation. Rice bran can be used for bran edible oil, husk can support biomass co-generation energy, ash, silica, blocks and other industrial applications. Research and investment can also explore rice straw-based boards, packaging materials, yarn and other products.

In Pakistan, however, rice straw is frequently burnt in fields, husk accumulates at rice mills, and valuable byproducts remain underutilised. At a time when the country urgently needs higher exports, rural employment, affordable energy and import substitution, this represents a substantial missed opportunity.

Beyond subsidies and penalties

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has launched a subsidy under the Punjab Clean Air Programme, offering rice growers Rs5,000 per acre, subject to a maximum of Rs25,000 per farmer, to discourage stubble burning. The initiative provides immediate assistance, but financial incentives alone cannot establish a permanent solution. Similarly, imposing fines on farmers and FIRs without providing practical and economically viable alternatives are unlikely to eliminate the problem sustainably. Pakistan needs to transform stubble management from a pollution-control exercise into a commercially viable agricultural industry.

Waste-to-Wealth Company

The Punjab government should establish an Agricultural Waste-to-Wealth Company to develop an integrated system for collecting, processing and marketing agricultural residues, beginning with rice straw and husk. Its principal responsibilities should include:

1-Rice-straw collection network: Establish collection centres in major rice-producing districts and provide balers, shredders and transportation through cooperatives and private contractors. Farmers should receive commercially viable prices for usable straw, creating a financial incentive to stop burning it. Collection operations must be organised around the short interval between rice harvesting and the planting of the next crop. Timely removal is essential if farmers are to adopt alternative practices.

2-Industrial utilisation and value addition: Encourage rice mills to utilise paddy husk for biomass power generation and industrial heat where economically feasible. Develop composting and organic-fertiliser facilities, and promote rice straw-based boards, packaging materials and other suitable manufactured products. Research institutions and businesses should investigate advanced applications, including biofuels and cellulose-based products. Where technically and commercially viable, cellulose extracted from rice straw could provide raw material for industrial applications, potentially including textile fibres and yarn. The objective should be to develop multiple uses for agricultural residues rather than depend on a single technology or market.

3-Private-sector investment: Invite domestic and foreign investors' joint ventures to establish agricultural waste processing facilities in rice-producing regions. The government should offer transparent, time-bound incentives linked to actual production, investment and verified residue utilisation. Long-term supply agreements between farmers, collection companies, rice mills and industrial consumers would help establish reliable supply chains and reduce commercial uncertainty.

4-Farmer participation and mechanisation: Farmers must be partners in the proposed system, not merely the targets of enforcement. Machinery for chopping, collecting, baling and transporting straw should be made accessible through service providers, cooperatives and affordable financing. Financial institutions, including Zarai Taraqiati Bank Limited and Apna Kissan Bank, could support eligible investments in agricultural machinery, collection centres, storage facilities and residue-processing projects. The government should aid coordination among agricultural departments, rice mills, research institutions and trade associations to ensure that collection and processing systems operate efficiently.

From agricultural waste to economic value

An integrated waste-to-wealth system could deliver several benefits simultaneously. These include reducing open-field burning and helping mitigate seasonal air pollution, generating additional income for rice farmers, creating rural employment and new businesses, supplying raw materials to energy and manufacturing industries, encouraging investment in agricultural technology, reducing waste and supporting import substitution, and developing new products with potential for domestic sales and exports.

However, success will depend on suitable technology, transport costs, reliable buyers and the economics of individual applications. Not all rice straw can be collected or processed profitably. Local feasibility studies and pilot projects should therefore precede large-scale investment. Punjab and Sindh should adapt their approaches to local agricultural conditions, infrastructure and industrial demand. The objective should be to establish commercially sustainable systems rather than create permanent dependence on subsidies.

Role of trade associations

Trade associations also have a responsibility beyond lobbying for their members' immediate demands. They should help develop the research, technology and industrial capabilities needed to make entire sectors more competitive. Pakistan's rice industry offers an opportunity to build clusters around agricultural residues, including straw, husk, bran and other byproducts. Such industries could diversify revenue streams, strengthen rural economies and improve the sector's overall competitiveness. After 79 years of independence, Pakistan needs less ceremonial and more economic leadership: laboratories instead of excessive ceremony, technology instead of trophy sales, and measurable results instead of publicity.

Stubble management must evolve from a policy focused primarily on controlling burning into a comprehensive resource-recovery industry. The government should facilitate investment, establish collection infrastructure, support research and create a regulatory environment in which agricultural waste becomes a commercially valuable resource. Farmers should earn from residues that currently impose disposal costs, while businesses should have incentives to convert them into marketable products. Pakistan's next rice revolution should not be measured solely by how much rice the country grows or exports, but by how much additional value it creates from every ton, and how little it wastes.

The writer is a former vice president of Karachi Chamber of Commerce & Industry and former board member of REAP

headline: The direct tax illusion
description: The direct tax illusion
author: Dr Ikramul Haq
article_text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has rediscovered an uncomfortable truth: Pakistan's tax system punishes those already documented while leaving powerful interests comparatively undisturbed. Its regional director, Jihad Azour, has called for fairness, neutrality and predictability. These are welcome words. The real test is whether the Fund and the government will examine what the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) actually collects, rather than what it chooses to call the collection.

The latest fiscal operations present an apparently encouraging picture. During 2025-26, the FBR collected Rs13.010 trillion, equivalent to 10.3% of gross domestic product (GDP). Of this, Rs6.586 trillion was classified as direct taxes: 5.19% of GDP against 5.05% a year earlier. Our examination of the finance ministry's July-June statements over 25 years confirms that this reported ratio is relatively high by historical standards, but extremely poor by international standards. It would be factually wrong to call it the lowest in a quarter-century. The failure lies elsewhere: the ratio increasingly conflates income taxation with collection on transactions and gross receipts.

The FBR's own mode-of-collection figures expose an alarming distortion. Of approximately Rs6.577 trillion recorded as income tax in 2025-26, Rs3.654 trillion came through withholding and another Rs2.208 trillion through advance payments under Section 147 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Payments accompanying returns supplied Rs250 billion. Thus, 92.9% came through these channels, compared with only 7.1% recovered out of demand. Assessment-based collection has improved, but remains a small fraction of the whole.

Withholding itself is not objectionable. Salary deductions, for example, can represent genuine taxation of income. The deception begins when levies on imports, contracts, electricity, telephone connections, exports and property transactions are advertised as proof of effective progressive income taxation.

Minimum and presumptive taxes on turnover can fall even where there is little profit, or a loss. Their legal classification does not establish who ultimately bears their economic burden; some may be passed into prices, depending on markets and contracts.

Our September 2026 briefing for the World Bank estimated that, after separating such transaction-linked and presumptive collections, the defensible measure of taxation of actual net income is around 3% of GDP and below 4%. This is an analytical estimate, not an independently audited official series. Comparable adjusted figures are unavailable for all 25 years. Nevertheless, the gap between 5.19% officially reported and approximately 3% economically estimated is too substantial to ignore.

The inequity is unmistakable. As The Express Tribune reported, salaried taxpayers paid Rs629 billion by June 2026, against Rs391 billion before the present IMF programme. Meanwhile, only 137 additional retailers had entered the designated scheme by October 15 against an annual target of one million. Provincial agricultural income tax receipts remained meagre. These figures demand scrutiny of implementation, exemptions and enforcement, not another indiscriminate squeeze on compliant citizens.

Pakistan needs to replace collection-point coercion with a credible system that taxes real incomes and demonstrable capacity to pay. Publish, separately, normal income tax, adjustable withholding, minimum and final taxes, assessed demands, and refunds due and paid. Bring untaxed wealth and valuable property into an administratively sound framework; protect modest livelihoods. Replace excessive rates and arbitrary advance deductions with broad, low, predictable taxation, meaningful audit and enforceable taxpayer rights.

The administrative record points to another failure. Tax authorities celebrate advance payments as voluntary compliance although those payments are mandated by statute. Counting return payments alongside automated deductions obscures the distinction between reporting income, paying on account and having taxable profits verified.

Equally, a tax collected by a bank or an importer may be legally adjustable later but still impose an immediate financing cost, especially where refunds are delayed. The system thereby penalises the documented enterprise twice: first through compliance costs, then through immobilised working capital. Real reform requires reconciliation of each deduction with the final liability, timely cash refunds and a transparent record of disputed demands. That is an institutional challenge, not merely a question of raising rates.

The IMF should insist on this transparency before congratulating the FBR on rising 'direct taxes'. A tax system is not equitable because a ledger says so. After decades of withholdingisation, the measure of success must be the income actually assessed, fairly taxed and honestly accounted for; not the amount extracted before income is even determined.

The writer is the Advocate Supreme Court, Adjunct Faculty at Lahore University of Management Sciences, member Advisory Board and Visiting Senior Fellow of PIDE

Of this, Rs6.586 trillion was classified as direct taxes: 5.19% of GDP against 5.05% a year earlier. Our examination of the finance ministry's July-June statements over 25 years confirms that this reported ratio is relatively high by historical standards, but extremely poor by international standards. It would be factually wrong to call it the lowest in a quarter-century. The failure lies elsewhere: the ratio increasingly conflates income taxation with collection on transactions and gross receipts.

The FBR's own mode-of-collection figures expose an alarming distortion. Of approximately Rs6.577 trillion recorded as income tax in 2025-26, Rs3.654 trillion came through withholding and another Rs2.208 trillion through advance payments under Section 147 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Payments accompanying returns supplied Rs250 billion. Thus, 92.9% came through these channels, compared with only 7.1% recovered out of demand. Assessment-based collection has improved, but remains a small fraction of the whole.

Withholding itself is not objectionable. Salary deductions, for example, can represent genuine taxation of income. The deception begins when levies on imports, contracts, electricity, telephone connections, exports and property transactions are advertised as proof of effective progressive income taxation.

Minimum and presumptive taxes on turnover can fall even where there is little profit, or a loss. Their legal classification does not establish who ultimately bears their economic burden; some may be passed into prices, depending on markets and contracts.

Our September 2026 briefing for the World Bank estimated that, after separating such transaction-linked and presumptive collections, the defensible measure of taxation of actual net income is around 3% of GDP and below 4%. This is an analytical estimate, not an independently audited official series. Comparable adjusted figures are unavailable for all 25 years. Nevertheless, the gap between 5.19% officially reported and approximately 3% economically estimated is too substantial to ignore.

The inequity is unmistakable. As The Express Tribune reported, salaried taxpayers paid Rs629 billion by June 2026, against Rs391 billion before the present IMF programme. Meanwhile, only 137 additional retailers had entered the designated scheme by October 15 against an annual target of one million. Provincial agricultural income tax receipts remained meagre. These figures demand scrutiny of implementation, exemptions and enforcement, not another indiscriminate squeeze on compliant citizens.

Pakistan needs to replace collection-point coercion with a credible system that taxes real incomes and demonstrable capacity to pay. Publish, separately, normal income tax, adjustable withholding, minimum and final taxes, assessed demands, and refunds due and paid. Bring untaxed wealth and valuable property into an administratively sound framework; protect modest livelihoods. Replace excessive rates and arbitrary advance deductions with broad, low, predictable taxation, meaningful audit and enforceable taxpayer rights.

The administrative record points to another failure. Tax authorities celebrate advance payments as voluntary compliance although those payments are mandated by statute. Counting return payments alongside automated deductions obscures the distinction between reporting income, paying on account and having taxable profits verified.

Equally, a tax collected by a bank or an importer may be legally adjustable later but still impose an immediate financing cost, especially where refunds are delayed. The system thereby penalises the documented enterprise twice: first through compliance costs, then through immobilised working capital. Real reform requires reconciliation of each deduction with the final liability, timely cash refunds and a transparent record of disputed demands. That is an institutional challenge, not merely a question of raising rates.

The IMF should insist on this transparency before congratulating the FBR on rising 'direct taxes'. A tax system is not equitable because a ledger says so. After decades of withholdingisation, the measure of success must be the income actually assessed, fairly taxed and honestly accounted for; not the amount extracted before income is even determined.

The writer is the Advocate Supreme Court, Adjunct Faculty at Lahore University of Management Sciences, member Advisory Board and Visiting Senior Fellow of PIDE

Its regional director, Jihad Azour, has called for fairness, neutrality and predictability. These are welcome words. The real test is whether the Fund and the government will examine what the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) actually collects, rather than what it chooses to call the collection.

The latest fiscal operations present an apparently encouraging picture. During 2025-26, the FBR collected Rs13.010 trillion, equivalent to 10.3% of gross domestic product (GDP). Of this, Rs6.586 trillion was classified as direct taxes: 5.19% of GDP against 5.05% a year earlier. Our examination of the finance ministry's July-June statements over 25 years confirms that this reported ratio is relatively high by historical standards, but extremely poor by international standards. It would be factually wrong to call it the lowest in a quarter-century. The failure lies elsewhere: the ratio increasingly conflates income taxation with collection on transactions and gross receipts.

The FBR's own mode-of-collection figures expose an alarming distortion. Of approximately Rs6.577 trillion recorded as income tax in 2025-26, Rs3.654 trillion came through withholding and another Rs2.208 trillion through advance payments under Section 147 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Payments accompanying returns supplied Rs250 billion. Thus, 92.9% came through these channels, compared with only 7.1% recovered out of demand. Assessment-based collection has improved, but remains a small fraction of the whole.

Withholding itself is not objectionable. Salary deductions, for example, can represent genuine taxation of income. The deception begins when levies on imports, contracts, electricity, telephone connections, exports and property transactions are advertised as proof of effective progressive income taxation.

Minimum and presumptive taxes on turnover can fall even where there is little profit, or a loss. Their legal classification does not establish who ultimately bears their economic burden; some may be passed into prices, depending on markets and contracts.

Our September 2026 briefing for the World Bank estimated that, after separating such transaction-linked and presumptive collections, the defensible measure of taxation of actual net income is around 3% of GDP and below 4%. This is an analytical estimate, not an independently audited official series. Comparable adjusted figures are unavailable for all 25 years. Nevertheless, the gap between 5.19% officially reported and approximately 3% economically estimated is too substantial to ignore.

The inequity is unmistakable. As The Express Tribune reported, salaried taxpayers paid Rs629 billion by June 2026, against Rs391 billion before the present IMF programme. Meanwhile, only 137 additional retailers had entered the designated scheme by October 15 against an annual target of one million. Provincial agricultural income tax receipts remained meagre. These figures demand scrutiny of implementation, exemptions and enforcement, not another indiscriminate squeeze on compliant citizens.

Pakistan needs to replace collection-point coercion with a credible system that taxes real incomes and demonstrable capacity to pay. Publish, separately, normal income tax, adjustable withholding, minimum and final taxes, assessed demands, and refunds due and paid. Bring untaxed wealth and valuable property into an administratively sound framework; protect modest livelihoods. Replace excessive rates and arbitrary advance deductions with broad, low, predictable taxation, meaningful audit and enforceable taxpayer rights.

The administrative record points to another failure. Tax authorities celebrate advance payments as voluntary compliance although those payments are mandated by statute. Counting return payments alongside automated deductions obscures the distinction between reporting income, paying on account and having taxable profits verified.

Equally, a tax collected by a bank or an importer may be legally adjustable later but still impose an immediate financing cost, especially where refunds are delayed. The system thereby penalises the documented enterprise twice: first through compliance costs, then through immobilised working capital. Real reform requires reconciliation of each deduction with the final liability, timely cash refunds and a transparent record of disputed demands. That is an institutional challenge, not merely a question of raising rates.

The IMF should insist on this transparency before congratulating the FBR on rising 'direct taxes'. A tax system is not equitable because a ledger says so. After decades of withholdingisation, the measure of success must be the income actually assessed, fairly taxed and honestly accounted for; not the amount extracted before income is even determined.
The writer is the Advocate Supreme Court, Adjunct Faculty at Lahore University of Management Sciences, member Advisory Board and Visiting Senior Fellow of PIDE

headline: French, Pakistani cultures meet via food in Karachi
description: French, Pakistani cultures meet via food in Karachi
author: Qaisar Kamran
article_text:
French cuisine is taking centre stage in Karachi as the Alliance Française de Karachi launches the 2026 edition of Good France / Goût de France, bringing together restaurants, chefs and food enthusiasts to celebrate French gastronomy and cultural exchange.

The week-long celebration, running from 31 October to 8 November, opened with a gala dinner at Avari Towers on Saturday, featuring visiting French chef Maxime Delaboudinière, who travelled from Paris to prepare a five-course meal for guests.

Organised by the Alliance Française de Karachi with the support of the French Embassy in Pakistan, the event also brings five local restaurants Cote Rotie, PAUL Bakery & Cafe, Feyaa, Okra and Olive Tree Bistro, on board. They will offer specially curated French-inspired menus during French Gastronomy Week, from 1 to 8 November.

Speaking to The Express Tribune, Alliance Française de Karachi Director Emmanuel Breurec said the initiative was about more than introducing French food to Pakistani diners; it was also an opportunity to build connections between the two cultures.

"As the director of the French Cultural Centre here, we have exchanges with Pakistani artists and French artists, and what links us is the love of exchanges. We share French culture and are curious about Pakistani culture," he said.

Breurec added that visiting chefs and artists offered opportunities for people from both countries to learn from one another.

"Every time an artist or a chef, for example, comes here, he is going to meet a Pakistani artist or Pakistani chef. We love to exchange culture," he said.

The visiting chef, Delaboudiniere, brings nearly two decades of experience in the restaurant industry. He currently serves as executive chef and director of Restaurant Duvin, a Parisian bistro, and has previously led kitchens at several restaurants in the French capital.

First launched in 2015 by France's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and renowned chef Alain Ducasse, Good France is an international initiative celebrating French cuisine and its place in global culinary culture.

In the 14th century, Guillaume Tirel, a court chef known as "Taillevent", wrote Le Viandier, one of the earliest recipe collections of medieval France. In the 17th and 18th centuries, chefs François Pierre La Varenne and Marie-Antoine Carême spearheaded movements that shifted French cooking away from its foreign influences such as from Italian cuisine and developed France's own indigenous style.

Cheese and wine are a major part of the cuisine. They play different roles regionally and nationally, with many variations and appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC) (regulated appellation) laws.

Culinary tourism and the Guide Michelin helped to acquaint commoners with the cuisine bourgeoise of the urban elites and the peasant cuisine of the French countryside starting in the 20th century. Many dishes that were once regional have proliferated in variations across the country.

Knowledge of French cooking has contributed significantly to Western cuisines. Its criteria are used widely in Western cookery school boards and culinary education. In November 2010, French gastronomy was added by the UNESCO to its lists of the world's "intangible cultural heritage".

French cuisine continues to change and adapt. In the contemporary period. "La Bistronomie" describing a fusion of bistro and haute cuisine emerged alongside new popular foods such as the French taco, new styles of food including food trucks, growing interest in vegetarian food and increased vegetarian options, and a public interest in simpler dining options. These changes are alongside the incorporation and mainstreaming of dishes from immigrant communities in part shaped by immigration and global exchange. Culinary influences are especially strong from across the Francophone world and beyond, including North African cuisines (notably couscous, which is often cited as one of modern France's most widely consumed dishes), Lebanese cuisine (with foods like falafel becoming widely popular), Southeast Asian traditions from countries such as Vietnam and Cambodia (including pho and banh mi), and a growing presence of African cuisines and spices in everyday French cooking. This transformation is tied to the French restaurant workforce with immigrants playing a major role in French commercial kitchens. Estimates suggest roughly twenty-five percent of chefs in France are immigrants, and in Paris about half of chefs are immigrants. France also continues to attract international chefs to train, who either stay in France or return to their home countries after learning French techniques.

The Karachi edition aims to bring that tradition closer to local audiences while creating opportunities for culinary and cultural exchange between France and Pakistan.

headline: Shae Gill, Afusic explore love, heartbreak
description: Shae Gill, Afusic explore love, heartbreak
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Coke Studio Nu.WAV has brought together Shae Gill and Afusic for its fifth release, Qasam, an experimental pop track that explores the emotional complexities of a relationship caught between love, hurt and uncertainty.

Produced and directed by Abdullah Kasumbi, the song combines electronic production with the traditional sound of the sarangi, played by Gul Khan. Written by Afusic, Qasam explores the struggle of holding on to a relationship despite emotional distance and the possibility of separation.

The track brings a different musical dimension to both performers. While Afusic retains his familiar rhythmic delivery, Shae Gill experiments with a vocal style that audiences have heard less frequently from her. Their contrasting voices add to the song's emotional character.

The accompanying music video takes a movement-led approach to storytelling, with choreography by Shams Mansur reflecting the changing dynamics between two people. Dancers appear connected by invisible strings, drawing closer and moving apart, while other sequences use movements resembling stitches to suggest a relationship repeatedly breaking and coming together.

Shot at Karachi's century-old Bristol Hotel, the video uses the building's ageing interiors, chandeliers and weathered surfaces to establish its visual atmosphere. Production designer Hammad Sohail also incorporates fading flowers and an untouched banquet table into the setting.

Another central image is the moth drawn towards a flame, inspired by the Sufi metaphor of shama and parwana. The symbolism reflects the attraction and emotional risks at the heart of the relationship.

Speaking about the release, Coke Studio Nu.WAV executive producer Kamal Khan said the song and video developed together under Kasumbi's creative direction, allowing the music, choreography and visual elements to form a unified world.

For Shae Gill, the release follows her breakthrough with Pasoori, alongside Ali Sethi, while Afusic returns to the platform after appearing on its opening track, Dil. His song Pal Pal also gained international attention, reaching the UK Official Asian Music Chart and Canada's Hot 100.

Shae Gill rose to prominence after her world-famous Punjabi-Urdu duet song "Pasoori" with Ali Sethi, in Coke Studio season 14. This song brought her immense popularity from around the world. She started her career as a cover-artist on Instagram in 2019. She mainly posted cover songs on Instagram.

Qasam is the fifth of six releases from Coke Studio Nu.WAV, following Dil, Rangeen, Maheya and Shabnam.

article_html:
KARACHI:

Coke Studio Nu.WAV has brought together Shae Gill and Afusic for its fifth release, Qasam, an experimental pop track that explores the emotional complexities of a relationship caught between love, hurt and uncertainty.

Produced and directed by Abdullah Kasumbi, the song combines electronic production with the traditional sound of the sarangi, played by Gul Khan. Written by Afusic, Qasam explores the struggle of holding on to a relationship despite emotional distance and the possibility of separation.

The track brings a different musical dimension to both performers. While Afusic retains his familiar rhythmic delivery, Shae Gill experiments with a vocal style that audiences have heard less frequently from her. Their contrasting voices add to the song's emotional character.

The accompanying music video takes a movement-led approach to storytelling, with choreography by Shams Mansur reflecting the changing dynamics between two people. Dancers appear connected by invisible strings, drawing closer and moving apart, while other sequences use movements resembling stitches to suggest a relationship repeatedly breaking and coming together.

Shot at Karachi's century-old Bristol Hotel, the video uses the building's ageing interiors, chandeliers and weathered surfaces to establish its visual atmosphere. Production designer Hammad Sohail also incorporates fading flowers and an untouched banquet table into the setting.

Another central image is the moth drawn towards a flame, inspired by the Sufi metaphor of shama and parwana. The symbolism reflects the attraction and emotional risks at the heart of the relationship.

Speaking about the release, Coke Studio Nu.WAV executive producer Kamal Khan said the song and video developed together under Kasumbi's creative direction, allowing the music, choreography and visual elements to form a unified world.

For Shae Gill, the release follows her breakthrough with Pasoori, alongside Ali Sethi, while Afusic returns to the platform after appearing on its opening track, Dil. His song Pal Pal also gained international attention, reaching the UK Official Asian Music Chart and Canada's Hot 100.

Shae Gill rose to prominence after her world-famous Punjabi-Urdu duet song "Pasoori" with Ali Sethi, in Coke Studio season 14. This song brought her immense popularity from around the world. She started her career as a cover-artist on Instagram in 2019. She mainly posted cover songs on Instagram.

Qasam is the fifth of six releases from Coke Studio Nu.WAV, following Dil, Rangeen, Maheya and Shabnam.

headline: Performing arts take centre stage at World Culture Festival
description: Performing arts take centre stage at World Culture Festival
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The fourth day of the 3rd World Culture Festival Karachi 2026, organised by the Arts Council of Pakistan Karachi, featured a diverse range of cultural activities, including the musical masterclass "VIOLA & CELLO", screening of the Pakistani film Wakhri, theatre performance "Chicha", musical programme "Crossfade" and dance showcase "Beats Galore".

The day began with an international music masterclass conducted by the renowned group ALIF DUO, representing the United Arab Emirates, South Korea and France. Titled "Strings, Harmony and Counterpoint", the session offered participants practical musical training. Artists Seulki Lee and Antonin Le Faure introduced participants to the technical skills involved in playing the violin, viola and cello. They also highlighted various aspects of Western classical music, musical harmony and interplay.

During the workshop, Antonin Le Faure said that he had studied music from Asian, African and other countries. He emphasised that curiosity was essential to learning music, adding that every note had its own significance and purpose. He said that music could only truly be learned when it was felt.

Seulki Lee observed that even the slightest change in a musical note could be distinctly perceived. She said artificial intelligence (AI) could never replace this profession, as music was a means of expressing human emotions. Artists and music students from various countries participated in the masterclass with great enthusiasm.

The festival also featured a screening of the Pakistani film Wakhri, which drew a large audience. Following the screening, director Eram Parveen Bilal joined the discussion via video link, while producer Abid Merchant participated in person. The discussion covered various aspects of the film, with audience members also taking part in a question-and-answer session.

The theatre group Grieta Teatro from Uruguay presented "Chicha", featuring a solo performance by artist Betina Andarina. The distinctive physical theatre and clowning performance used music, body movements and memories to explore human emotions, silence and stories of the past. The 45-minute performance combined acting and music to make the audience laugh, evoke emotions and reflect on the true meaning of being human.

The international musical programme "CROSSFADE" brought together artists from Japan, France, Pakistan and Serbia. Juna Serita from Japan, Zakaria Haffar from France, Asteria from Pakistan and Aleksander from Serbia showcased their musical talents. Their distinctive musical styles and captivating melodies entertained the audience.

The fourth day concluded with "Beats Galore", a vibrant dance showcase featuring outstanding performances by international artists. The participating performers included Valerie Green from the USA; Josh Middleton and Rebecca Solomon from the UK; Away Runakuna from Ecuador; Cia Livre de Dança da Rocinha from Brazil; Sherene Joseph from Singapore; and Tina Zubovic and SOVAPA Students from Croatia. The performances, reflecting diverse cultures and distinctive dance styles, captivated the audience.

The auditorium echoed with applause as the artists received enthusiastic appreciation. It remained packed throughout the programme, with the international performances earning widespread acclaim.

It is worth mentioning that the World Culture Festival features more than 1,000 international artists from over 150 countries, alongside more than 500 Pakistani artists, showcasing their talents. The 25-day festival presents a wide range of cultural activities, including theatre, music, dance and visual arts, highlighting the cultures, artistic expressions and traditions of people from around the world.

The World Culture Festival will continue at the Arts Council of Pakistan Karachi until November 22, with the public able to attend through free registration.

headline: Governor pledges K-P's first right to resources
description: Governor pledges K-P's first right to resources
author: Wisal Yousafzai
article_text:
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Sunday said the province's people would have the "first right" to its natural resources, pledging that their interests would remain his priority while he held office.

Addressing a ceremony in Peshawar, Kundi said the province was rich in natural resources, including gas, minerals, electricity and oil.

"My first priority is the protection of the people. As long as I hold this office, the first right over our resources will belong to the people of our province," he said.

Kundi said residents of K-P had made immense sacrifices in the fight against terrorism, adding that restoring peace required collective efforts. "Although we may have differences on many issues, we must stand united to establish peace in the province," he said.

He said the province had suffered from terrorism for a long time, with schoolchildren, security forces, police personnel and journalists among those who had made countless sacrifices for peace.

"Our mission is to make the province a cradle of peace," he said.

The governor highlighted that his first priority was to restore peace. He added that the people of the province had distinguished themselves in various fields, adding that more than half of the national cricket team's players belonged to K-P. "We have immense talent in the field of sports," he said.

Kundi also urged religious scholars to play their role in promoting peace, saying people listened to and respected their views.

He said children wanted to lead full and peaceful lives, while residents sought opportunities for business and employment.

"It is our shared responsibility to play our full part in the development, prosperity and peace of the province," he said, adding that the government would welcome constructive suggestions for improving the province and its cities.

The governor also pledged to work with all stakeholders to bring peace, prosperity and development to K-P.

Mineral rights

On October 11, Governor's rule and an emergency were imposed, transferring executive authority from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf-led provincial government to the governor. An 11-member advisory council was formed to assist him in overseeing provincial administrative affairs.

headline: Pakistan's polio tally reaches eight with new case in K-P
description: Pakistan's polio tally reaches eight with new case in K-P
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The National Emergency Operations Centre (NEOC) for Polio Eradication confirmed Pakistan's seventh polio case of the year, reported from Khyber district of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P).

The affected child is a 13-month-old girl belonging to Jan Baz Union Council in Bara tehsil, the NEOC said. This is the second polio case reported from Khyber district this year and the sixth from K-P.

Of the seven cases reported across the country so far this year, six have emerged from K-P and one from Sindh, according to the NEOC.

The centre said polio was an incurable disease but could be prevented through vaccination.

A special anti-polio campaign will begin on Monday (Nov 2) in 97 selected districts across the country and continue until Nov 8, the NEOC said.

During the sub-national immunisation campaign, more than 24 million children under the age of five would be administered polio drops.

The NEOC urged parents to ensure their children received polio drops during every campaign and completed their routine immunisation schedules on time.

It also appealed to all segments of society to play their role in eliminating polio from the country.

Pakistan has reduced polio cases by 99.8%, according to the NEOC. The estimated number of cases fell from around 20,000 in the early 1990s to 31 in 2025. Seven cases have been reported so far this year.

According to the NEOC, Pakistan has conducted four large-scale polio vaccination campaigns this year, targeting more than 45 million children. These efforts have been complemented by smaller, targeted oral and injectable vaccination campaigns in high-risk areas.

A subnational campaign in September vaccinated more than 29.3 million children across the country, the NEOC said.

headline: PMDC clears 99% of doctor registrations
description: PMDC clears 99% of doctor registrations
author: Razya Khan
article_text:
The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) has successfully issued 302,587 registrations out of 304,819 applications received across various categories, clearing more than 99% of the total applications up to October 2026 through improvements to its registration system and administrative procedures.

Under the leadership and direction of its president Prof. Dr Rizwan Taj, the council has taken proactive measures to strengthen its registration mechanism, ensuring faster processing, prompt disposal of cases and more efficient handling of applications submitted by doctors and dental professionals.

Through improved workflow management, proactive monitoring and greater attention to pending cases, the council has worked to ensure that applications are processed efficiently and applicants receive timely responses.

A key achievement of these measures has been the facilitation of doctors without requiring unnecessary visits to the PMDC office.

By improving the handling of registration-related matters through its online portal and better administrative coordination, the council has enabled medical and dental professionals to complete their cases remotely, saving valuable time, reducing travel expenses and minimising inconvenience.

This has been particularly beneficial for doctors serving in hospitals, remote areas and other demanding professional settings.

The latest figures demonstrate the council's efforts to address the growing demand for registration and verification services through its digital registration portal.

With the continuous upgrading of its registration system and proactive monitoring, the PMDC has focused on improving registration operations through closer oversight of application volumes, processing status, objections and pending cases.

headline: Stampede at TikToker's mehndi kills two, injures 17
description: The crowd had gathered at the ground for the mehndi ceremony of the popular TikToker
author: Ghazanfar Warraich
article_text:
A prize draw at a TikToker's wedding celebration turned deadly after a stampede at Faraz Ground in Daska left two people dead and 17 others injured, prompting Sialkot police to register a case against the event organiser, TikToker Ansar Jatt, alias 'Mr Patlu', and several others.

The crowd had gathered at the ground for the mehndi ceremony of the popular TikToker, who had announced a prize draw featuring cars, motorcycles and cash rewards to attract participants and publicise the event.

The rush at the entrance gate triggered a stampede, during which several people fell to the ground and were trampled underfoot.

One of the victims, Aqeel, a resident of Budha Goraya, died at the scene, while 18 people were initially injured and shifted to hospitals. Among the injured was Rehan, a resident of Glotian Kalan, whose condition was critical.

He was referred to Lahore's Mayo Hospital but later succumbed to his injuries, taking the death toll to two and leaving 17 others injured.

Soon after receiving information about the incident, Sialkot District Police Officer Captain (retd) Dost Muhammad reached the site. Police and Rescue 1122 personnel jointly shifted the injured to hospitals and cleared routes to facilitate the movement of ambulances.

Police registered a case at Motra police station on their own complaint under Sections 322, 431, 440, 188, 109, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with Section 16 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO).

FIR names nine people, including event organiser Ansar Mahmood, alias 'Mr Patlu', Kashif, ground owner Haji Shahid Javed and other organisers Daniyal, Munir Ahmed, Mohsin Ali, Irshad Ali, Abdullah and Zohaib Mansha. Another 40 to 45 unidentified security guards have also been included in the case.

Police conducted raids late at night and arrested six suspects, while efforts were underway to apprehend the main accused, 'Mr Patlu', and the remaining suspects.

The funeral prayers of both victims were offered in their respective ancestral villages, where they were laid to rest in the presence of hundreds of mourners.

Meanwhile, the district administration said an NOC had been issued for holding a mehfil-e-samaa and qawwali night at the private event, which was scheduled to take place after Isha prayers.

headline: K-P council faces operational delays
description: The 48-member council was established to oversee government affairs in 12 districts where an emergency was imposed
author: Ahtesham Bashir
article_text:
The 48-member council was established to oversee government affairs in 12 districts where an emergency was imposed

The Area Representatives and Development Council (ARDC), established for 12 districts of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), has yet to become fully operational more than two weeks after its formation, with its secretariat and offices still not functioning.

The 48-member council was established to oversee government affairs in 12 districts where an emergency was imposed on October 11 amid a PTI protest.

These include Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, Upper South Waziristan, Lower South Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat and Bannu.

Former K-P governor Shaukatullah Khan has been appointed chairman of the council.

A separate secretariat has also been established for the 12 districts and placed in charge of 32 departments, for which separate secretaries have been appointed. The old Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) Secretariat building on Warsak Road has been allocated for the purpose.

However, more than two weeks after the council's formation, offices have not been allocated to the departments and the administrative setup remains incomplete. The government had also decided to establish councils at the tehsil level, but their members have not yet been selected.

headline: Terror attacks in country drop by 37% in October
description: Terror attacks in country drop by 37% in October
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan recorded a 37 per cent decline in terrorist attacks in October, offering a temporary respite after two consecutive months of rising violence, although a sharp increase in kidnappings, particularly in Balochistan, continued to pose a serious security challenge.

According to statistics released by the Islamabad-based Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), 143 terrorist attacks were recorded across the country during October, compared with 226 in September.

The reduction was accompanied by a 57 per cent fall in fatalities and a 71 per cent decline in injuries. The improvement was particularly noticeable in Balochistan and mainland Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, while suicide attacks also registered a substantial decrease.

PICSS data showed that the attacks claimed 111 lives in October, compared with 260 in September. The number of people injured dropped from 242 to 69, indicating a 71 per cent reduction.

The overall human cost of violence, including terrorist attacks and counterterrorism operations by security forces, comprised 53 security personnel, 45 civilians and five peace committee members killed, while 169 terrorists were also killed, according to the report.

The 69 people injured in terrorist attacks included 29 security forces personnel, 11 peace committee members and 31 civilians.

The number of suicide attacks was jointly the lowest recorded during the same period. However, the 169 terrorists killed also represented the lowest monthly figure in the preceding 12 months, reflecting a decline in terrorist fatalities, the report noted.

Suicide attacks fell sharply in October, with only one incident recorded against three in September. The October incident involved a vehicle-borne suicide attack but caused no fatalities or injuries.

In comparison, the three suicide attacks in September, including two vehicle-borne attacks, claimed 45 lives and left 138 people injured. Consequently, fatalities and injuries resulting from suicide attacks both declined by 100 per cent in October.

Meanwhile, counterterrorism operations conducted by security forces across the country resulted in the killing of 156 terrorists and the arrest of seven suspected terrorists during October. Two security personnel and three civilians were killed in these operations, while two security forces personnel were injured.

Balochistan registered one of the sharpest improvements in its security indicators, with terrorist attacks falling by 46 per cent, from 132 in September to 71 in October.

Mainland Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, excluding the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), also witnessed a considerable decline in terrorist violence.

PICSS recorded 40 attacks in the region during October, compared with 58 in September, marking a reduction of 31 per cent. Deaths resulting from these attacks fell from 90 to 38, a decline of around 58 per cent, while injuries dropped sharply from 165 to 19, representing an 88 per cent decrease.

Punjab recorded two terrorist attacks in October, compared with none in September. The incidents left four people dead, while no injuries were reported.

Sindh witnessed no terrorist attacks during the month. However, counterterrorism operations in the province led to the arrest of seven suspected terrorists.

headline: PMD forecasts dry weather across country
description: PMD forecasts dry weather across country
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
.

The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) has forecast dry weather across most parts of the country over the next 24 hours, with partly cloudy skies and cold conditions expected in northern areas.

Light rain and snowfall over hills are likely at isolated places in upper Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan during the night, the department said.

The minimum temperatures recorded in major cities on Sunday morning were 24 degrees Celsius in Karachi, 17 in Lahore, 14 in Peshawar, 12 in Islamabad, 11 in Muzaffarabad, nine in Quetta and eight each in Gilgit and Murree.

headline: PUC chief urges Muslim unity
description: PUC chief urges Muslim unity
author: APP
article_text:
.

Pakistan Ulema Council (PUC) Chairman Tahir Ashrafi has called upon Muslim countries to set aside their differences, strengthen mutual cooperation and forge a united strategy to address regional and international challenges.

Addressing a conference on Sunday, he said collective efforts are essential for peace, stability and security across the Muslim world. He said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are playing an important role in bringing Muslim countries closer.

He said Israel, India and their allies are pursuing designs to destabilise the Muslim world, stressing that unity and collective action are necessary to counter such challenges.

headline: China pushes Pakistan ties beyond government
description: China pushes Pakistan ties beyond government
author: Kamran Yousaf
article_text:
A senior Chinese Communist Party official responsible for managing the party's international political relations arrived in Islamabad on Sunday for his first official visit to Pakistan.

This move underscores Beijing's efforts to deepen political and institutional engagement with Islamabad beyond traditional government-to-government diplomacy.

Liu Haixing, minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, is visiting Pakistan at the invitation of Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. During his stay, he is scheduled to call on Pakistan's leadership and co-chair a high-level event with Dar on Monday (today).

Announcing the visit, the Foreign Office said it was part of the ongoing high-level and party-to-party exchanges between the two countries, reflecting their shared commitment to further strengthening the "All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership".

The visit comes in a landmark year for bilateral relations, as Pakistan and China are marking the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties.

It also follows Dar's meeting with Liu in Beijing in January, when the two sides reviewed party-to-party exchanges, regional developments and progress on various projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) project.

According to the Foreign Office, both sides expressed satisfaction with the "steady and forward-looking trajectory" of bilateral relations and agreed to commemorate the anniversary in a befitting manner.

Liu's position in the Chinese political system gives the visit significance beyond conventional diplomatic engagement.

Unlike officials of China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he heads a key department of the Communist Party responsible for maintaining relations with political parties and political organisations across the world.

Founded in 1951, the International Department serves as the CPC's principal channel for party-to-party diplomacy. It maintains contacts with ruling and opposition parties, facilitates political exchanges and provides a platform for discussing governance, development and international affairs.

The department operates within the Communist Party's institutional structure rather than the Chinese government's Foreign Ministry. Its role is therefore distinct from conventional diplomatic engagement, although both channels work within the broader foreign policy direction set by China's leadership.

Liu is a member of the 20th CPC Central Committee and was appointed head of the International Department in September 2025. A career diplomat, he previously served as assistant foreign minister and director-general of the Foreign Ministry's Department of European Affairs.

Before taking up his current assignment, he served as executive vice-director of the General Office of the CPC Central Committee's National Security Commission, an important party body chaired by President Xi Jinping.

article_html:
ISLAMABAD:

A senior Chinese Communist Party official responsible for managing the party's international political relations arrived in Islamabad on Sunday for his first official visit to Pakistan.

This move underscores Beijing's efforts to deepen political and institutional engagement with Islamabad beyond traditional government-to-government diplomacy.

Liu Haixing, minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, is visiting Pakistan at the invitation of Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. During his stay, he is scheduled to call on Pakistan's leadership and co-chair a high-level event with Dar on Monday (today).

Announcing the visit, the Foreign Office said it was part of the ongoing high-level and party-to-party exchanges between the two countries, reflecting their shared commitment to further strengthening the "All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership".

The visit comes in a landmark year for bilateral relations, as Pakistan and China are marking the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties.

It also follows Dar's meeting with Liu in Beijing in January, when the two sides reviewed party-to-party exchanges, regional developments and progress on various projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) project.

According to the Foreign Office, both sides expressed satisfaction with the "steady and forward-looking trajectory" of bilateral relations and agreed to commemorate the anniversary in a befitting manner.

Liu's position in the Chinese political system gives the visit significance beyond conventional diplomatic engagement.

Unlike officials of China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he heads a key department of the Communist Party responsible for maintaining relations with political parties and political organisations across the world.

Founded in 1951, the International Department serves as the CPC's principal channel for party-to-party diplomacy. It maintains contacts with ruling and opposition parties, facilitates political exchanges and provides a platform for discussing governance, development and international affairs.

The department operates within the Communist Party's institutional structure rather than the Chinese government's Foreign Ministry. Its role is therefore distinct from conventional diplomatic engagement, although both channels work within the broader foreign policy direction set by China's leadership.

Liu is a member of the 20th CPC Central Committee and was appointed head of the International Department in September 2025. A career diplomat, he previously served as assistant foreign minister and director-general of the Foreign Ministry's Department of European Affairs.

Before taking up his current assignment, he served as executive vice-director of the General Office of the CPC Central Committee's National Security Commission, an important party body chaired by President Xi Jinping.

headline: Afghan terror havens: Marco Rubio opens door to US role
description: Afghan terror havens: Marco Rubio opens door to US role
author: News Desk
article_text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a press briefing on Saturday said Washington had "obviously heard" Pakistan's concerns regarding terrorism emanating from Afghan soil, adding that "if there's a productive role for us to play, we'll play it."

"Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan," Rubio said, addressing a briefing in Atlanta, Georgia. He added that Islamabad felt "as though the Taliban have not done enough to constrain those attacks and they've taken action against it."

The secretary of state added, "We obviously have heard those concerns on their part, we obviously don't want them to be targeted."

He also noted that Washington didn't "necessarily have the closest relationship with the Taliban," but that "we've heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we've seen some of those attacks that they point to."

Rubio concluded, "We're against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets."

His remarks came amid strained relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan due to recurring cross-border terrorism and security concerns. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Afghan Taliban administration to prevent terrorist organisations, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), from using its territory to launch attacks inside Pakistan.

Islamabad has rejected Taliban assurances that Afghan territory would not be used against neighbouring countries, arguing that the ground situation and documented militant activity tell a different story.

Pakistan maintains that the terrorist nexus extended beyond the movement of terrorists across the border to their training, arming and operational support.

Security officials estimate that up to 70% of the Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists infiltrating Pakistan were of Afghan origin.

headline: FCC reasserts its status as apex court
description: FCC reasserts its status as apex court
author: Hasnaat Malik
article_text:
In a judgement that elaborates the scope of review as well as its appellate jurisdiction, the newly established Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has again asserted its superiority, stating that Supreme Court judgements are not binding on it, although they can carry "persuasive value".

"The judgments of the Supreme Court are not binding on us, but carry persuasive value and where the jurisprudence laid down by it appeals or seems to be in consonance with the law and the Constitution, may be followed," said an 8-page judgement authored by Justice Aamer Farooq.

A three-member bench led by Justice Farooq while hearing a review petition also said that Supreme Court jurisprudence evolved for leave to appeal from the decisions/orders of the high court under Article 199 of the Constitution is also not binding on it.

However, the FCC noted that it can draw wisdom from Supreme Court jurisprudence.

The judgement also noted that the crux of the jurisprudence on the subject is that the review jurisdiction of this court is quite limited and is circumscribed; being confined to the errors apparent on the face of the record or mistakes/shortcomings which would result in the miscarriage of justice.

"Recent trends show that litigants/lawyers treat review jurisdiction as another opportunity to reargue the case; by no means while hearing a review application the bench is rehearing the matter, it is only to see if there is an apparent error/mistake on the face of the record.

"Rule 4 of Order XXVII of the Rules clearly provides that the Advocate-on-Record (AOR) or the party, along with the review application shall append a certificate, in the form of a reasoned opinion, stating that, in the opinion of the AOR or the party, as the case may be, the application is maintainable and that a review is justified in accordance with the law and the practice of the court."

The order said that the party or the AOR should exercise utmost care in handing down the certificate or opining on the issue as wrong certificate can have grave repercussions.

It reiterated that the practice to file a review application as a matter of course, wherein the ground(s) for review are not attracted, does not find favour with this court and is deprecated inasmuch as mostly the review applications are nothing but a rehearing of the matter.

The FCC expected the litigants and legal community to exercise caution and file review applications only in cases where it is genuinely felt that the grounds are attracted.

"The reason we are expressing in lucid manner the caution which the party and AOR is to exercise is because of the ramifications provided in the Rules with respect to frivolous and vexatious review applications.

"In this behalf, under the Rules where the court comes to the conclusion that review application is frivolous or vexatious, it can impose costs of not less than Rupees 25,000 or the AOR can be susceptible to disciplinary proceedings, as well (Rule 5(a) of the Rules)"

Likewise, the judgement said that where there is no legal representation and the court comes to the conclusion that the application is vexatious or frivolous, the party shall be liable to costs of not less than Rs25,000.

"No application for review is to be entertained, as per Rule 6 of the Rules, unless the applicant deposits a sum of Rupees 50,000/- as security in the designated account of the court.

"Rule 6(2) empowers the court to forfeit the sum deposited as security, if the review application is dismissed or found to be frivolous or vexatious.

"Since review is an extraordinary jurisdiction in the sense that the grounds on which it can be filed are too restricted, this court, in appropriate cases, may dispose of a review application by circulation without oral hearing, unless it considers that a hearing is essential."

The court notes that the sole purpose of citing all the relevant rules pertaining to the review jurisdiction of this court is only to sensitize the litigants and the legal fraternity about its constricted scope and the consequences provided in the rules for frivolous and vexatious applications.

Regarding the concept of the jurisdiction under Article 175F(1)(c), the order said that the party has to obtain permission or leave of the court for its appeal to be heard.

"Prior to the incorporation of Article 175F(1)(c) in the Constitution through the 27th (Constitutional Amendment) Act, 2025, this jurisdiction was exercised by the Supreme Court under Article 185(3) of the Constitution.

"After the abovementioned constitutional amendment, this court was created and its appellate jurisdiction, inter alia, included hearing petitions for leave to appeal from the decisions/orders of the High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution.

"The jurisprudence which the Supreme Court of Pakistan evolved, in this regard, which is not binding on us but wisdom can be drawn from it, is that leave can only be allowed if there is any question of law in the matter or indulgence is required to prevent miscarriage of justice."

Comparing with Indian SC jurisprudence, the judgement noted that the jurisprudence evolved with respect to adjudicating the petitions for leave to appeal is perhaps different in Pakistan and definitely has parameters.

"By no means is a petition for leave to appeal an appeal as of right and only if leave is allowed then the petition acquires the status of appeal and is to be heard like one.

"When the court dismisses the application/petition for leave to appeal, it does not necessarily endorse the order against which leave is sought.

"While adjudicating a leave application, the court is not required to give reasons for its decision. If the court is of the view that no case for grant of leave is made out, it can hold so simply through a non-speaking order.

"Like-wise, while allowing leave to appeal the same can be done without a speaking order," the FCC stated.
